translation_en:
…whatever the people detested, they took every care to guard against it. Repelling threats from without was itself the cultivation of good government within. Those in the outer domains were like those in the inner domains: who would disobey commands from above and cast himself beyond the king’s transforming influence? Awe of his majesty was itself affection for his virtue. Those in large states were like those in small states: who would act contrary to established norms and incur the condemnation of royal law? Ah! Here we can see the comprehensive unity of the Zhou king’s government. Yet King Cheng succeeded Kings Wen and Wu, whose plans and achievements remained fully intact; surely there were none who failed to acknowledge his court. The campaign against the Huai Yi was confined to a single corner of the realm: how, then, could there be talk of campaigns in all four directions? In recording King Cheng’s early government, the court historian showed both his resolve never to forget danger amid security and the transforming influence of a true king, which leaves no one outside its reach. Ah! With the Offices of Zhou to instruct the hundred officials, all—from the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries down to the ministers and regional governors—had their regular duties: the personnel for government were fully provided. With the Rituals of Zhou to govern all under Heaven, all—from the royal court to the various states—had their regular rites: the institutions of government were complete. With both personnel and institutions fully provided, was this not why the Zhou dynasty enjoyed its rule for so long?

Classic of Odes
“Heaven gave birth to the multitude of people; for every thing there is a norm. The people hold fast to their constant nature and love this admirable virtue.”
Wang Honghui 王弘誨

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: This topic concerns the study of human nature and principle. Those writing on it in the examination hall are either superficial or dry. This essay expounds it in plain, natural language, flowing so abundantly that scarcely any deeper meaning remains unexpressed…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
其深造而有得者歟
同考試官教諭曾批發則與彞德處精潤透
徹可與語心學矣
考試官教諭黃批善發性情之蘊□心理
者
考試官學正宋批至微之理文足以發
詩人原天之生人性善而情亦善也蓋性命於
天而情發乎性本無不善也天之所以生人者
固如此哉昔尹吉甫作詩以送仲山甫而推其
===
所由生也若曰明於天之道者斯可以言性察
於民之故者斯可以言情求之生人之初而知
天之所以篤生賢哲矣是故天之生烝民也太
極儲其精未有物先而此理爲之不息二五凝
其化既有物後而此理爲之各具由氣而生者
必有主乎氣者畀之以昭當然之極蓋時有古
今而此無虧欠也依形而立者必有形而上者
付之以植天然之中蓋人有智愚而此無豐嗇
也是物則也帝降之衷本之於有生之初而恒
banxin: 天台鄉試錄 三十六
punctuated:
其深造而有得者歟？

同考試官教諭曾批：發則與彞德處，精潤透徹，可與語心學矣。

考試官教諭黃批：善發性情之蘊，□心理者。

考試官學正宋批：至微之理，文足以發。

詩人原天之生人，性善而情亦善也。蓋性命於天，而情發乎性，本無不善也。天之所以生人者，固如此哉！昔尹吉甫作詩以送仲山甫，而推其所由生也，若曰：明於天之道者，斯可以言性；察於民之故者，斯可以言情。求之生人之初，而知天之所以篤生賢哲矣。是故天之生烝民也，太極儲其精，未有物先，而此理爲之不息；二五凝其化，既有物後，而此理爲之各具。由氣而生者，必有主乎氣者畀之，以昭當然之極，蓋時有古今，而此無虧欠也；依形而立者，必有形而上者付之，以植天然之中，蓋人有智愚，而此無豐嗇也。是物則也，帝降之衷，本之於有生之初，而恒
translation_en:
…Might he be one who has pursued learning deeply and attained understanding for himself?

Associate Examiner Zeng, Instructor, comments: His exposition of the standards and of constant virtue is refined, polished, and penetrating. He is someone with whom one may discuss the learning of the mind.

Examiner Huang, Instructor, comments: He ably brings out the hidden depths of human nature and the feelings—[?] the mind and principle.

Examiner Song, Director of Studies, comments: His writing is adequate to disclose the subtlest principles.

The poet traces Heaven’s generation of human beings to its source: human nature is good, and the feelings are also good. For human nature is ordained by Heaven, while the feelings issue from that nature; originally, neither contains anything that is not good. Surely this is how Heaven generates human beings! Formerly, Yin Jifu composed a poem to send off Zhong Shanfu and traced the source of his birth. It is as though he said: Only those who understand Heaven’s Way can speak of human nature; only those who discern the circumstances of the people can speak of the feelings. By seeking at the very beginning of human generation, one comes to understand how Heaven brings forth worthy and wise men in particular abundance.

Thus, when Heaven generates the multitude of the people, the Supreme Ultimate stores up its essence: before things exist, this principle operates ceaselessly. The two forces and five phases—yin and yang and the Five Phases—consolidate their transformations: once things exist, this principle is fully present in each. Whatever is born through material force must be endowed with something that governs that force, thereby making manifest the ultimate standard of what ought to be. Though times differ between antiquity and the present, this suffers no deficiency. Whatever stands by virtue of physical form must be endowed with something beyond physical form, thereby establishing its Heaven-given mean. Though people differ in wisdom and foolishness, this is neither more abundant nor more scant. These are the standards inherent in things. The inner norm bestowed by the Lord on High is rooted in the very beginning of life, and the constant…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
性在焉原於天而不可易者備於已而不可離
也繼善之理得之為固有之良而成性存焉命
之流行而不已者性之一定而不移也非民之
秉彝乎是以至德中涵旣原天下之一而無有
不善故循性而動自統天下之同而無不好善
好爵之縻根心而不容已理與心融未有人而
不好是德者其諸天下之達德乎理義之悅同
然而無所間心與理契未有懿德而人不好之
者其諸人情之大順乎兹見性情之善賦予之
===
公夫人之同得於天者而山甫獨全美德此所
以異於凡民歟雖然心統性情者也惟能善事
其心然後是非好惡出於性情自無不正此大
較也仲山甫小心翼翼大本已端故能不茹不
吐保身事君職業備舉以光中興偉業而為當
時之賢佐也吉甫之言不為無助矣故曰寫此
詩者其知道乎
我受命溥將自天降康豐年穰穰
鍾維藩
punctuated:
性在焉。原於天而不可易者，備於已而不可離也。繼善之理，得之為固有之良，而成性存焉。命之流行而不已者，性之一定而不移也。非民之秉彝乎？是以至德中涵，旣原天下之一而無有不善，故循性而動，自統天下之同而無不好善。好爵之縻，根心而不容已，理與心融，未有人而不好是德者，其諸天下之達德乎？理義之悅，同然而無所間，心與理契，未有懿德而人不好之者，其諸人情之大順乎？兹見性情之善，賦予之公。夫人之同得於天者，而山甫獨全美德，此所以異於凡民歟？雖然，心統性情者也。惟能善事其心，然後是非好惡出於性情，自無不正，此大較也。仲山甫小心翼翼，大本已端，故能不茹不吐，保身事君，職業備舉，以光中興偉業，而為當時之賢佐也。吉甫之言，不為無助矣。故曰：「寫此詩者，其知道乎？」

我受命溥將，自天降康，豐年穰穰。

鍾維藩
translation_en:
…nature inheres therein. What originates in Heaven and cannot be altered is fully present in oneself and cannot be separated from oneself. The principle whose continuation is goodness is received as one's inherent goodness, and therein resides the nature brought to completion. What flows unceasingly as Heaven's mandate is fixed and unchanging as human nature. Is this not the constant norm that the people hold? Thus, consummate virtue is contained within: since it derives from the unity underlying all under Heaven, there is nothing in it that is not good. Consequently, when people act in accordance with their nature, their actions embrace what all under Heaven share, and none fails to love goodness. The attachment to noble rank [?] is rooted in the heart and cannot be restrained. Principle and the heart are fused; no person fails to love this virtue. Is this not the universal virtue of all under Heaven? The delight taken in principle and righteousness is shared alike, without distinction. The heart accords with principle; there is no admirable virtue that people do not love. Is this not the great harmony of human feelings? Here we see the goodness of human nature and feelings, and the impartiality of Heaven's endowment.

Now, this is something that everyone alike receives from Heaven, yet Shanfu alone fully possessed excellent virtue. Is this what distinguished him from ordinary people? Nevertheless, it is the heart that governs both nature and feelings. Only when one can properly attend to one's heart will the judgments of right and wrong, and the likes and dislikes, issuing from one's nature and feelings invariably be correct. This is the essential point. Zhong Shanfu was cautious and reverent, and his great foundation was already rightly established. Thus he neither swallowed the weak nor spat out the strong: he preserved his person and served his ruler, fulfilling all the duties of his office. In this way he brought lustre to the great achievement of dynastic restoration and became a worthy assistant of his age. Jifu's words are therefore not without benefit. Hence the saying: “Did not the writer of this poem understand the Way?”

“I have received the mandate, vast and great; from Heaven well-being descends; abundant harvests yield grain in profusion.”

Zhong Weifan

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭蕭批受命降康處都是得天
是篇以此貫說甚有照應且詞藻煥發盛世之音
也取式多士
同考試官教諭曾批題意正大士子多□陳
言束縛未見發明是作清暢脫俗塲中少見錄之
考試官教諭黄批語明意盡善作頌者
考試官學正宋批文思雋永且得詩人口
氣
商王膺天眷之隆而獲有年之慶此祀典之由
===
秩也夫君德莫大於得天也商王祀事之所由
備者何莫而非天之所與哉此祀成湯之樂及
此若曰王者繼統而御世也固天命之所歸而
備物以用享也亦天休之所及蓋商之先后受
命固不殆矣使不得乎天亦不敢以祭也今則
保玆世序而景命之有僕者以一人而統其盛
克享天心而駿命之不易者以一身而會其全
臨君師之任而貴爲天子所以主鬯而殷薦者
此也昭受于天不旣廣乎紹神明之統而富有
punctuated:
同考試官教諭蕭批：「受命、降康處，都是得天。是篇以此貫說，甚有照應，且詞藻煥發，盛世之音也，取式多士。」

同考試官教諭曾批：「題意正大，士子多□陳言束縛，未見發明。是作清暢脫俗，塲中少見，錄之。」

考試官教諭黄批：「語明意盡，善作頌者。」

考試官學正宋批：「文思雋永，且得詩人口氣。」

商王膺天眷之隆，而獲有年之慶，此祀典之由秩也。夫君德莫大於得天也，商王祀事之所由備者，何莫而非天之所與哉？此祀成湯之樂及此，若曰：王者繼統而御世也，固天命之所歸；而備物以用享也，亦天休之所及。蓋商之先后受命，固不殆矣；使不得乎天，亦不敢以祭也。今則保玆世序，而景命之有僕者，以一人而統其盛；克享天心，而駿命之不易者，以一身而會其全。臨君師之任，而貴爲天子，所以主鬯而殷薦者，此也。昭受于天，不旣廣乎？紹神明之統，而富有
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: “The passages on ‘receiving the mandate’ and ‘blessings descending’ both concern winning Heaven’s favor. This essay carries that idea throughout its exposition, with very effective internal correspondences. Moreover, its language is brilliant—the voice of a flourishing age. Let the many candidates take it as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zeng, Instructor: “The meaning of the topic is upright and grand. Most candidates are [?] constrained by conventional expressions and offer no elucidation. This composition is lucid, fluent, and free of commonplace language—a rarity in the examination hall. Record it.”

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “The language is clear and the meaning fully expressed: this is someone skilled at composing hymns of praise.”

Comment by Examiner Song, School Instructor: “The literary conception has lasting savor, and the essay also captures the poet’s voice.”

The king of Shang received Heaven’s abundant favor and enjoyed the blessing of a plentiful harvest; thus the sacrificial observances came to be duly ordered. Of a ruler’s virtues, none is greater than winning Heaven’s favor. How could anything that enabled the king of Shang to provide fully for the sacrifices have been other than Heaven’s gift? The music for the sacrifice to Cheng Tang reaches this point as if to say: when a king succeeds to the ruling line and governs the world, he is indeed the one upon whom Heaven’s mandate devolves; when he assembles the offerings for sacrifice, this too is the reach of Heaven’s blessing. For the former rulers of Shang received the mandate, assuredly without peril; yet had they not won Heaven’s favor, they would not have dared to sacrifice.

Now, preserving this succession through the generations, he gathers in his single person the full splendor of the great mandate so amply bestowed. Able to enjoy Heaven’s favor, he brings together in his single person the entirety of the mighty mandate, which is not easily maintained. He assumes the responsibilities of ruler and teacher and holds the exalted rank of Son of Heaven: this is what enables him to preside over the fragrant sacrificial wine and present abundant offerings. Is not what he has manifestly received from Heaven extensive indeed? He succeeds to the sacred line and possesses in abundance …

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
四海所以假廟而萃渙者此也靈承于帝不既
大乎夫我之受命固溥將矣使年不順成亦難
乎其成享也兹則天心仁愛而太和之氣布濩
於兩間厚之以明昭之賜帝命不違而絪縕之
化徧及於庶彙畀之以大有之祥我田既臧普
美利於不言而黍稷介倉箱之富則夫載清酤
而賚思成者其將有攸賴乎我稼既同示豐亨
於有象而收成極萬億之多則夫戒和羹而綏
眉壽者其將有所資乎夫受命之隆是天與之
===
使之主祭也降康之裕是天與之得以備物也
由是而假先獲福也固其所哉抑成湯敬德享
天已非一日而桑林數語尤足以綿亳都命脉
之長故奕世發祥豐年疊見脩禮作樂致力於
廟祊上下洽神人聲靈所振天地為昭而玄王
之緒賴以不墜何者而非先澤之所留也噫頌
明德歸功於祖受明命求端於天若湯孫者其
察於天人之道也歟
春秋
punctuated:
四海，所以假廟而萃渙者，此也。靈承于帝，不既大乎？夫我之受命，固溥將矣；使年不順成，亦難乎其成享也。兹則天心仁愛，而太和之氣布濩於兩間，厚之以明昭之賜；帝命不違，而絪縕之化徧及於庶彙，畀之以大有之祥。我田既臧，普美利於不言，而黍稷介倉箱之富，則夫載清酤而賚思成者，其將有攸賴乎？我稼既同，示豐亨於有象，而收成極萬億之多，則夫戒和羹而綏眉壽者，其將有所資乎？夫受命之隆，是天與之使之主祭也；降康之裕，是天與之得以備物也。由是而假先獲福也，固其所哉！抑成湯敬德享天，已非一日，而桑林數語，尤足以綿亳都命脉之長。故奕世發祥，豐年疊見，脩禮作樂，致力於廟祊，上下洽神人。聲靈所振，天地為昭，而玄王之緒賴以不墜，何者而非先澤之所留也？噫！頌明德，歸功於祖；受明命，求端於天。若湯孫者，其察於天人之道也歟！

春秋
translation_en:
…the Four Seas: this is what enables him to enter the ancestral temple and gather together what is dispersed. Is not his wondrous reception of the Lord on High’s favor great indeed? The mandate we have received is certainly vast and mighty; yet if the year’s crops did not ripen favorably, it would still be difficult to complete the sacrificial offering. Now, however, Heaven’s heart is benevolent and loving, and the vital energy of supreme harmony spreads throughout the space between Heaven and Earth, enriching us with its radiant gifts. The decree of the Lord on High does not fail, and the transforming interaction of vital forces reaches every kind of being, granting us the auspicious blessing of a great harvest. Our fields are good: fine benefits spread without a word being spoken, and millet fills granaries and carts with abundant wealth. Thus, when we set out clear wine and receive the fulfillment of our prayers, will we not have something on which to rely? Our crops have all ripened together: abundance and prosperity appear in visible form, and the harvest reaches countless myriads. Thus, when we prepare the seasoned broth and receive the blessing of long life, will we not have the means to do so? The exalted mandate is Heaven’s gift, enabling the ruler to preside over the sacrifices; the abundance of well-being bestowed upon him is Heaven’s gift, enabling him to provide the full range of offerings. That he should thereby approach his ancestors and receive blessings is surely fitting!

Moreover, Cheng Tang had long revered virtue and made offerings to Heaven, and his few words at Sanglin were especially sufficient to prolong the lifeblood of the capital at Bo. Thus, auspicious blessings arose generation after generation, and bountiful years appeared repeatedly. Rituals were cultivated and music composed; efforts were devoted to the ancestral temple and its precincts, bringing harmony among spirits and people above and below. Wherever this numinous authority exerted its power, Heaven and Earth shone forth, and through it the legacy of the Dark King was preserved from decline. Which of these things was not a lasting gift of ancestral beneficence? Ah! In praising radiant virtue, they credited their ancestors; in receiving the illustrious mandate, they sought its source in Heaven. Surely descendants of Tang such as these understood the Way of Heaven and humanity!

Spring and Autumn Annals

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
秋及江人黄人伐陳僖公四年
馬象乾
同考試官教諭翟批此題會合兩傳以見齊
桓之得失作者牽制文義難於竣整是篇渾融精
切且有斷制宜錄之以式多士
考試官教諭黄批得聖人予奪之旨
考試官學正宋批體裁正大
伯主用遠國以討貳春秋善其謀而病其德也
此齊於江黄用以制楚則善用以虐陳則非也
===
而功過不相掩矣且轅濤塗倡避軍之謀申侯
行師老之譛齊桓所為怒也乃率江黄以伐之
夫伐陳而後動二國之兵前此未之與也何以
為驗其謀也蓋用師之道貴萬全而取勝故有
正有奇法之所以為善也彼楚之陵駕中華也
得非以江黄與國為之捍蔽矣乎齊欲制楚而
非此以為掎角之資吾見厚集之衆雖當其前
八國之師孰援其後二廣之雄未可以遽帖也
惟其申以陽谷之好授以按兵之寄迨夫盟禮
punctuated:
秋，及江人、黄人伐陳。僖公四年。
馬象乾
同考試官教諭翟批：此題會合兩傳，以見齊桓之得失。作者牽制文義，難於竣整。是篇渾融精切，且有斷制，宜錄之以式多士。
考試官教諭黄批：得聖人予奪之旨。
考試官學正宋批：體裁正大。
伯主用遠國以討貳，春秋善其謀而病其德也。此齊於江黄，用以制楚則善，用以虐陳則非也，而功過不相掩矣。且轅濤塗倡避軍之謀，申侯行師老之譛，齊桓所為怒也，乃率江黄以伐之。夫伐陳而後動二國之兵，前此未之與也，何以為驗其謀也？蓋用師之道，貴萬全而取勝，故有正有奇，法之所以為善也。彼楚之陵駕中華也，得非以江黄與國為之捍蔽矣乎？齊欲制楚，而非此以為掎角之資，吾見厚集之衆雖當其前，八國之師孰援其後？二廣之雄，未可以遽帖也。惟其申以陽谷之好，授以按兵之寄，迨夫盟禮
translation_en:
“In autumn, we joined the men of Jiang and Huang in attacking Chen.” Fourth year of Duke Xi.
Ma Xianggan
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhai, Instructor: This topic brings together the two commentaries to reveal Duke Huan of Qi’s successes and failings. Writers are constrained by the meaning of the text and find it difficult to achieve a fully coherent composition. This essay is well integrated, precise, and incisive, and also offers decisive judgments. It should be recorded as a model for the candidates.
Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: It grasps the Sage’s intent in granting approval and withholding it.
Comment by Examiner Song, Instructor: Its form and style are correct and dignified.
The hegemon employed distant states to punish a wavering allegiance: the Spring and Autumn Annals approves his strategy but finds fault with his virtue. In Qi’s employment of Jiang and Huang, using them to restrain Chu was good, but using them to oppress Chen was wrong. His achievements and faults do not cancel one another out.
Yuan Taotu proposed a plan to divert the army, and Shen Hou slanderously alleged that it would exhaust the troops. This angered Duke Huan of Qi, who then led Jiang and Huang in attacking Chen. Yet he mobilized the troops of these two states only for the attack on Chen; previously they had not participated. How can this demonstrate his strategic skill? The way of employing armies prizes securing victory with complete assurance; hence there are both regular and extraordinary operations. This is what makes military methods effective. Was not Chu’s overbearing domination of the Central States due to its having the allied states of Jiang and Huang as a protective screen? If Qi wished to restrain Chu without employing these states to threaten it from different directions, then, as I see it, although massed forces might confront Chu from the front, who among the armies of the eight states would provide support at its rear? The might of Chu’s two chariot divisions could not readily be subdued. It was precisely because he renewed friendly relations at Yanggu and entrusted these states with holding their troops in readiness that, once the covenant ceremony…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之旣定然後連兵以伐陳則知侵蔡次陘之不
與者非不用夫江黃也羽翼方城之外使進焉
有所憑坐制漢水之境使退焉有所據伏至險
於大順藏不測於至靜兵法之奇將以待敵之
可勝者也斯非謀之成乎夫師老而後致不共
之問兵出非無名也何以為病其德也蓋持勝
之道貴克終而不替故有容有忍德之所以為
大也彼陳之謀避軍道也無乃以伯政無良莫
之攸思矣乎齊欲討陳而反己以省見斁之由
===
吾見愛人不親將以反仁治人不治將以反智
一謀之愆何至於大逞也夫何恣勝外之餘威
忘輔伯之舊好械執之辱未已撻伐之師繼之
其視勤鄭禮楚之不同者非偶拂其初心也志
溢於功成之後而弗克自持氣驕於克敵之餘
而莫能自抑包荒之量已淺容受之度不弘匡
救之仁假之不久而遽歸者也斯非德之衰乎
噫此一役也明於制楚而暗於懷陳桓之得失
如此宜其止於伯而不得進於王也抑考江黃
punctuated: 之旣定，然後連兵以伐陳，則知侵蔡次陘之不與者，非不用夫江黃也。羽翼方城之外，使進焉有所憑；坐制漢水之境，使退焉有所據。伏至險於大順，藏不測於至靜，兵法之奇，將以待敵之可勝者也。斯非謀之成乎？夫師老而後致不共之問，兵出非無名也，何以為病其德也？蓋持勝之道，貴克終而不替，故有容有忍，德之所以為大也。彼陳之謀避軍道也，無乃以伯政無良，莫之攸思矣乎？齊欲討陳，而反己以省見斁之由，吾見愛人不親，將以反仁；治人不治，將以反智。一謀之愆，何至於大逞也？夫何恣勝外之餘威，忘輔伯之舊好？械執之辱未已，撻伐之師繼之。其視勤鄭禮楚之不同者，非偶拂其初心也。志溢於功成之後，而弗克自持；氣驕於克敵之餘，而莫能自抑。包荒之量已淺，容受之度不弘，匡救之仁，假之不久而遽歸者也。斯非德之衰乎？噫！此一役也，明於制楚而暗於懷陳，桓之得失如此，宜其止於伯而不得進於王也。抑考江黃
translation_en:
…had been settled through the covenant rites, only then did they join forces to attack Chen. We can therefore see that Jiang and Huang’s nonparticipation in the invasion of Cai and the encampment at Xing did not mean that their forces were left unused. They served as supporting wings beyond Fangcheng, giving the advancing army something to rely upon; they held command over the region of the Han River, giving it a secure position to fall back upon. Concealing the utmost danger within complete conformity to the proper order, and hiding the unpredictable within perfect stillness: these were unconventional military methods, awaiting the moment when the enemy could be defeated. Was this not a success in planning?

Yet only after the army had grown weary did he call Chu to account for its failure to render tribute. The campaign was certainly not without a legitimate cause; why, then, do we regard it as a blemish on his virtue? The way to preserve victory prizes carrying matters through to the end without faltering. Thus it requires tolerance and forbearance: these are what make virtue great. As for Chen’s scheme to divert the army’s route away from itself, was this not perhaps because the hegemon’s government lacked goodness and gave no thought to Chen? Had Qi, when wishing to punish Chen, instead examined itself to discover why it was disliked, I believe it would have reflected upon its benevolence when its love for others elicited no affection, and upon its wisdom when its governance failed to bring order. How could the fault of a single scheme justify so unrestrained an assertion of power? Why indulge the lingering威勢 of victory abroad and forget the old friendship that had supported his hegemony? Before the humiliation of arrest in fetters had ended, a punitive army followed. The contrast with his solicitude for Zheng and his courteous treatment of Chu was no accidental departure from his original intentions. After success, his ambitions overflowed and he could no longer restrain himself; after defeating his enemies, his spirit grew arrogant and he could no longer hold himself in check. His capacity to embrace others’ shortcomings had diminished, and his tolerance was no longer broad. The benevolence with which he had set the world right and rescued it was something borrowed, soon returned. Was this not a decline in virtue?

Alas! In this one campaign, he understood how to check Chu but failed to understand how to win Chen’s allegiance. Such were Duke Huan’s successes and failures. It was fitting that he should attain only hegemony and be unable to advance to true kingship. Yet, if we examine Jiang and Huang…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
受盟管仲能鏡其終矣殊無一語以箴伐陳之
失豈其懵於此也蓋量淺之桓而仲以小器佐
之數年經營惟一楚耳召陵之後侈心生焉自
脩乏制心之學事君無格心之功宜誠僞勤怠
互異如此然一匡之績叔世賴焉聖人且以仁
稱之仲固不可多得也
春公孫歸父會楚子于宋宣公十有五年
闕玉成
同考試官教諭翟批發揮聖人經世之畧精
===
確顯明是深于經學者
考試官教諭黃批詞嚴義正
考試官學正宋批整飭有體
春秋志望國交外之迹所以示經世之略也此
觀魯之屈志以下楚其自治者疎矣春秋得無
譏乎昔楚師在宋虐焰張甚魯宣懼其及也乃
從獻子之謀遣歸父而爲宋之會君子所以譏
之者蓋以攘夷安夏匡時之偉略强本治内保
邦之良圖當時荆楚爲讎於大邦重兵横加于
punctuated:
受盟，管仲能鏡其終矣，殊無一語以箴伐陳之失，豈其懵於此也？蓋量淺之桓，而仲以小器佐之，數年經營，惟一楚耳。召陵之後，侈心生焉。自脩乏制心之學，事君無格心之功，宜誠僞勤怠互異如此。然一匡之績，叔世賴焉，聖人且以仁稱之，仲固不可多得也。
春，公孫歸父會楚子于宋。宣公十有五年。
闕玉成。
同考試官教諭翟批：發揮聖人經世之畧，精確顯明，是深于經學者。
考試官教諭黃批：詞嚴義正。
考試官學正宋批：整飭有體。
春秋志望國交外之迹，所以示經世之略也。此觀魯之屈志以下楚，其自治者疎矣，春秋得無譏乎？昔楚師在宋，虐焰張甚，魯宣懼其及也，乃從獻子之謀，遣歸父而爲宋之會。君子所以譏之者，蓋以攘夷安夏，匡時之偉略；强本治内，保邦之良圖。當時荆楚爲讎於大邦，重兵横加于
translation_en:
…accepted the covenant, Guan Zhong could foresee their eventual fate. Yet he offered not a single word to admonish against the error of attacking Chen. Could he have been unaware of this? Duke Huan was limited in his capacity, and Zhong assisted him with his own narrow abilities. Their years of planning concerned Chu alone. After Shaoling, an extravagant ambition arose. In cultivating himself, Zhong lacked the learning needed to govern his mind; in serving his ruler, he achieved nothing in rectifying the ruler’s mind. Little wonder that sincerity and pretence, diligence and indolence alternated in this way. Yet his achievement in setting the realm in order sustained an age of decline, and the Sage even praised him as benevolent. Men like Zhong were indeed hard to come by.
“In spring, Gongsun Guifu met the Viscount of Chu in Song.” The fifteenth year of Duke Xuan.
Que Yucheng.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhai, Instructor: “He expounds the Sage’s strategy for ordering the world with precision and clarity. This is someone deeply versed in classical learning.”
Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “The language is rigorous and the principles correct.”
Comment by Examiner Song, Schoolmaster: “Well ordered and properly structured.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals records the dealings of prominent states [?] with outside powers in order to reveal the strategy for ordering the world. Here we see Lu humbling its aspirations to submit to Chu: its management of its own affairs was deficient. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to censure it? Formerly, when Chu’s army was in Song and the flames of its cruelty burned fiercely, Duke Xuan of Lu feared that they would reach him. He therefore followed Xianzi’s advice and sent Guifu to hold the meeting in Song. The reason the gentleman censures this is that repelling the barbarians and securing the Xia states is the great strategy for putting the age to rights, while strengthening the foundations and governing internal affairs is the sound plan for preserving a state. At that time, Jing-Chu was acting as an enemy to the great states, wantonly directing its mighty army against…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
上國其目中已無諸夏矣此不獨當為宋人計
當為天下計也魯宣於此誠能擇義而行則畏
簡書以攘夷狄存先代於垂亡此其策之上也
如欲相時而動則嚴兵旅以為聲援消外患於
方張未為謀之失也奈何內政罔脩惟懷不免
之懼剥牀是慮遂忘下比之傷周公之裔義非
不明也以此制人何向而不克顧乏有為之志
未及而薦賄何其鄙也千乘之國力非不足也
以此備豫何敵之敢窺顧忽深長之思千里而
===
畏人何其陋也若曰庭實之獻以脩睦也然鄰
封告急乃以壇坫之好而往與亂華者同焉屈
我之體而示之弱使益肆其桀驁之威則將何
以待之若曰禮幣之交以行成也然四境無虞
乃以下敵之禮而遠於殘夏者施焉畏人之勢
而中之利使益恣其無厭之求又將何以應之
魯之君臣筭不及此何國之能為也吾知非惟
無以制楚也適以長楚憑陵之志非惟無以恤
宋也適以怠宋堅守之心夷夏盛衰之由蓋決
punctuated: 上國，其目中已無諸夏矣。此不獨當為宋人計，當為天下計也。魯宣於此誠能擇義而行，則畏簡書以攘夷狄，存先代於垂亡，此其策之上也。如欲相時而動，則嚴兵旅以為聲援，消外患於方張，未為謀之失也。奈何內政罔脩，惟懷不免之懼，剥牀是慮，遂忘下比之傷。周公之裔，義非不明也；以此制人，何向而不克？顧乏有為之志，未及而薦賄，何其鄙也！千乘之國，力非不足也；以此備豫，何敵之敢窺？顧忽深長之思，千里而畏人，何其陋也！若曰庭實之獻以脩睦也，然鄰封告急，乃以壇坫之好而往，與亂華者同焉，屈我之體而示之弱，使益肆其桀驁之威，則將何以待之？若曰禮幣之交以行成也，然四境無虞，乃以下敵之禮而遠於殘夏者施焉，畏人之勢而中之利，使益恣其無厭之求，又將何以應之？魯之君臣筭不及此，何國之能為也？吾知非惟無以制楚也，適以長楚憑陵之志；非惟無以恤宋也，適以怠宋堅守之心。夷夏盛衰之由，蓋決
translation_en:
…the states of the central realm; in its eyes, the various states of Xia already counted for nothing. This called for deliberation not merely on behalf of the people of Song, but on behalf of all under Heaven. Had Duke Xuan of Lu truly been able at this juncture to choose and act upon what was right, he would have heeded the written summons to duty, repelled the Yi and Di, and preserved the heirs of a former dynasty on the verge of extinction. This would have been his best strategy. If he wished instead to act according to the circumstances, he could have put his troops in readiness to provide support and checked the external menace as it was gathering strength. This, too, would have been no error in planning. Why, then, did he neglect internal government and harbor only the fear that he would not escape? Concerned solely that destruction would reach his very bed, he forgot the harm of basely attaching himself to another power. As a descendant of the Duke of Zhou, he was not ignorant of righteousness. Had he used it to restrain others, where could he have turned without success? Yet he lacked the resolve to act and offered gifts before the threat even reached him. How contemptible! As ruler of a state possessing a thousand war chariots, he did not lack strength. Had he used it to prepare his defenses, what enemy would have dared covet his territory? Yet he neglected far-reaching deliberation and feared another power a thousand li away. How narrow-minded!

One might say that the presentation of court gifts was intended to cultivate amity. Yet when a neighboring state appealed for urgent aid, he went instead to cultivate ceremonial friendship, joining with those who were throwing the Hua states into disorder. By lowering his own dignity and displaying weakness, he encouraged them to exercise their overbearing might still more freely. How, then, would he deal with them? One might say that the exchange of ceremonial gifts was intended to make peace. Yet when his own borders were free of danger, he extended, to a distant power ravaging the Xia states, the courtesies of submission to an enemy. By fearing its power and gratifying its desire for gain, he encouraged it to indulge its insatiable demands still further. How, then, would he answer them? If the ruler and ministers of Lu failed to reckon with these consequences, how could they govern a state? I know that this not only failed to restrain Chu, but positively encouraged Chu’s ambition to dominate and encroach; it not only failed to succor Song, but positively weakened Song’s determination to hold firm. What determined the rise and decline of the Yi and Xia was surely settled…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
於此矣聖人脩經至此蓋曰中國有常尊之體
則外勢自屈有常勝之謀則外侮自消治內以
馭外蓄威以奠邦斯非經世者所宜知乎直書
其事而義自見矣抑楚之橫晉成之也徇小利
而忽遠猷楚得以竊義自張矣桓文而在能無
少戢乎魯宣負惡而不能自固齊猶足以奔走
之欲其不惴於楚焉難矣然華元當危急而不
受城下之盟魯於無事乃切後時之虞何節槩
之相遠也君子於獻子有遺論矣其於宣也何
===
尤
禮記
故樂者天地之命中和之紀人情之所不
能免也
陳維翰
同考試官教諭曾 批 命紀必須融會體貼上
文作者不泛則繞此篇意盡而詞復警健可式
考試官教諭黃 批 詞意精確
考試官學正宋 批 明順
punctuated:
於此矣。聖人脩經至此，蓋曰：中國有常尊之體，則外勢自屈；有常勝之謀，則外侮自消。治內以馭外，蓄威以奠邦，斯非經世者所宜知乎？直書其事，而義自見矣。抑楚之橫，晉成之也。徇小利而忽遠猷，楚得以竊義自張矣。桓文而在，能無少戢乎？魯宣負惡而不能自固，齊猶足以奔走之，欲其不惴於楚焉，難矣。然華元當危急而不受城下之盟，魯於無事乃切後時之虞，何節槩之相遠也！君子於獻子有遺論矣，其於宣也何尤？

禮記

故樂者，天地之命，中和之紀，人情之所不能免也。

陳維翰

同考試官教諭曾，批：「命紀必須融會體貼上文，作者不泛則繞。此篇意盡而詞復警健，可式。」

考試官教諭黃，批：「詞意精確。」

考試官學正宋，批：「明順。」
translation_en:
…was determined at this point. When the Sage reached this point in compiling the Classic, his meaning was presumably this: if the central states maintain a consistently honored standing, outside powers will of themselves submit; if they possess plans that consistently secure victory, foreign aggression will of itself subside. Order affairs within to control those without; build up authority to secure the state. Is this not what those who govern the world ought to understand? He records the event directly, and its moral significance becomes apparent of itself. Moreover, it was Jin that enabled Chu’s overbearing conduct. By pursuing petty advantages and neglecting long-term plans, Jin allowed Chu to appropriate the mantle of righteousness and aggrandize itself. Had Dukes Huan and Wen been alive, could Chu have failed to show some restraint? Duke Xuan of Lu, burdened by wrongdoing, could not secure his own position. Even Qi could make him do its bidding; to expect him not to tremble before Chu would have been difficult. Yet Hua Yuan, in a moment of grave peril, refused a covenant imposed beneath his city’s walls, whereas Lu, when facing no emergency, was deeply anxious about acting too late. How far apart they were in integrity and resolve! Gentlemen have left their critical judgment of Xianzi; what further reproach need they direct at Duke Xuan?

Record of Rites (Liji)

“Thus music is the ordinance of Heaven and Earth, the ordering principle of equilibrium and harmony, and something human feelings cannot do without.”

Chen Weihan

Associate Examiner Zeng, Instructor, comments: “‘Ordinance’ and ‘ordering principle’ must be understood together and interpreted with close attention to the preceding text. Writers tend either to be vague or to become convoluted. This essay fully develops the meaning, while its language is also striking and vigorous. It can serve as a model.”

Examiner Huang, Instructor, comments: “Precise in both expression and meaning.”

Examiner Song, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Clear and fluent.”

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
論正樂之在人其功大而不可離也蓋人莫不
有天地中和之理也樂以命之紀之人情其得
而免乎樂記結言樂之切於人也曰人知凡樂
之動不能外乎情而不知人情之治實有資於
樂蓋嘗於其聲容之感化者而觀其深矣今夫
天地之賦於人者有曰親曰敬曰順之道焉樂
聲之作而因以廣之則德音之洋溢有以感觸
夫天性之眞中聲之揄揚有以啓發其秉彞之
懿以達其神以興其德而凡天地之所不及者
===
皆正樂以鼓舞之也樂非天地之命乎中和之
具於人者有曰莊曰正曰齊之儀焉樂舞之舉
而因以飭之則干羽之習合有以遠暴慢而攝
威儀綴兆之周旋有以黜邪僻而全恭敬以動
血脉以通精神而凡中和之在於吾身者皆正
樂以綱維之也樂非中和之紀乎夫樂爲天地
之命則致樂以治心而精粗相凝之體實平心
宣化之資樂爲中和之紀則致樂以治躬而情
文兼備之具爲志和行成之本養德養身而有
punctuated:
論正樂之在人，其功大而不可離也。蓋人莫不有天地中和之理也，樂以命之、紀之，人情其得而免乎？《樂記》結言樂之切於人也，曰：人知凡樂之動不能外乎情，而不知人情之治實有資於樂，蓋嘗於其聲容之感化者而觀其深矣。

今夫天地之賦於人者，有曰親、曰敬、曰順之道焉。樂聲之作而因以廣之，則德音之洋溢有以感觸夫天性之眞，中聲之揄揚有以啓發其秉彞之懿，以達其神，以興其德，而凡天地之所不及者，皆正樂以鼓舞之也。樂非天地之命乎？中和之具於人者，有曰莊、曰正、曰齊之儀焉。樂舞之舉而因以飭之，則干羽之習合有以遠暴慢而攝威儀，綴兆之周旋有以黜邪僻而全恭敬，以動血脉，以通精神，而凡中和之在於吾身者，皆正樂以綱維之也。樂非中和之紀乎？

夫樂爲天地之命，則致樂以治心，而精粗相凝之體，實平心宣化之資；樂爲中和之紀，則致樂以治躬，而情文兼備之具，爲志和行成之本。養德養身，而有
translation_en:
The argument concerns orthodox music as it operates in human beings: its efficacy is great, and it cannot be dispensed with. All people possess the principles of Heaven and Earth, equilibrium and harmony. Music gives these direction and order; how, then, could human feelings dispense with it? The Record of Music (Yueji) concludes by explaining how closely music concerns human beings. Its meaning is this: people know that every stirring produced by music necessarily involves feelings, but they do not know that ordering human feelings actually depends on music. If we consider how its sounds and outward forms move and transform people, we can perceive the depth of its influence.

What Heaven and Earth bestow upon human beings includes the ways of familial affection, reverence, and obedience. When musical sounds arise, these qualities are thereby enlarged. The overflowing of virtuous tones can stir the genuineness of our Heaven-endowed nature; the expressive unfolding of balanced sounds can awaken the excellence of our innate moral constants. Music thus gives expression to the spirit and rouses virtue. Wherever the work of Heaven and Earth does not reach, orthodox music supplies its animating influence. Is music not, then, the mandate of Heaven and Earth? Equilibrium and harmony, as embodied in human beings, include the forms of solemnity, rectitude, and dignified composure. When musical dances are performed, these are thereby regulated. Practice and coordination with shields and feather plumes can keep violence and arrogance at a distance and bring one's bearing under control. Turning and moving through the prescribed dance positions can banish perversity and preserve full respect and reverence. These stir the blood and vital channels and allow the vital spirit to circulate freely. All the equilibrium and harmony within our persons is thus held in order by orthodox music. Is music not, then, the ordering framework of equilibrium and harmony?

Since music is the mandate of Heaven and Earth, one brings music to its fullest realization to govern the heart. Its constitution, in which the subtle and the gross cohere, truly provides the means to bring peace to the heart and spread transforming influence. Since music is the ordering framework of equilibrium and harmony, one brings music to its fullest realization to govern one's person. As an instrument complete in both inward feeling and outward form, it is the foundation for harmonizing the will and perfecting conduct. It nourishes virtue and nourishes the person, and its presence…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
無關性術之理亂是日用之所必資焉者而可
以終身違哉成身成性而得失係志氣之安危
誠吾人之所必有事焉者而可以斯須去哉由
是而知正樂之感其化甚神而生民之道惟樂
爲大也先王立樂之方不其盡善盡美矣乎抑
君子於天地之命而見樂有盡性之功焉於中
和之紀而見樂有踐形之功焉踐形盡性樂之
於情甚切矣故曰禮樂之說管乎人情記者於
此可謂達樂之本矣作樂者夫苟不知天地中
===
和命紀之理而但求之文采節奏之間抑末矣
又安能感人動物之神速也哉故正樂之功於
是爲大
天子者與天地參故德配天地兼利萬物
林華
同考試官教諭曾批 題本明白正大場中士
子類能敷演成篇求其渾厚精粹者亦不多見錄
此以式
考試官教諭黃批 文理嚴整可誦
punctuated:
無關性術之理亂，是日用之所必資焉者，而可以終身違哉？成身成性，而得失係志氣之安危，誠吾人之所必有事焉者，而可以斯須去哉？由是而知正樂之感，其化甚神，而生民之道，惟樂爲大也。先王立樂之方，不其盡善盡美矣乎？抑君子於天地之命，而見樂有盡性之功焉；於中和之紀，而見樂有踐形之功焉。踐形盡性，樂之於情甚切矣。故曰：「禮樂之說，管乎人情。」記者於此，可謂達樂之本矣。作樂者夫苟不知天地中和命紀之理，而但求之文采節奏之間，抑末矣，又安能感人動物之神速也哉？故正樂之功，於是爲大。
天子者，與天地參，故德配天地，兼利萬物。
林華
同考試官教諭曾批：題本明白正大，場中士子類能敷演成篇，求其渾厚精粹者，亦不多見。錄此以式。
考試官教諭黃批：文理嚴整，可誦。
translation_en:
…or absence bears upon order or disorder in one's nature and conduct. This is something indispensable to daily life: how could one turn away from it throughout one's lifetime? In perfecting oneself and fulfilling one's nature, success or failure determines the stability or peril of one's resolve and vital energies. This is indeed something to which we must devote ourselves: how could we abandon it even for an instant? From this we know that the influence of proper music works transformations of wondrous subtlety, and that, among the ways of ordering human life, music is paramount. Were not the former kings' methods of establishing music perfectly good and perfectly beautiful? Moreover, in music as the mandate of Heaven and Earth, the gentleman perceives its efficacy in fully realizing one's nature; in music as the ordering framework of equilibrium and harmony, he perceives its efficacy in fulfilling one's bodily form. In fulfilling one's bodily form and fully realizing one's nature, music bears most closely upon human feelings. Thus it is said: “The teachings of ritual and music govern human feelings.” Here the compiler of the Record may be said to have comprehended the root of music. If those who create music do not understand the principles of Heaven and Earth, equilibrium and harmony, mandate and ordering framework, but seek it solely in ornamentation and rhythm, they pursue mere externals. How, then, could they influence people and move other beings with such wondrous speed? Hence the efficacy of proper music is great in these respects.
“The Son of Heaven forms a triad with Heaven and Earth; thus his virtue matches Heaven and Earth, and he benefits all things alike.”
Lin Hua

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正宋批〔順暢〕
聖君之合乎造化於其德業徵之矣夫德配天
地德之盛也兼利萬物業之大也天子如此其
參於天地也宜哉經解記孔子之言也嘗謂天
地之大也夫人難乎其參矣獨不觀聖人在天
子之位乎是故乾稱乎父坤稱乎母而大君則
宗子於其間天位乎上地位乎下而聖人則成
位於其中崇效卑法而神化以備仰觀俯察而
人極以立參乎天地者其惟天子也已矣蓋嘗
===
自其盛德大業而觀之今夫大哉至哉天地之
爲德固極盛而無以加矣惟天子者以一心涵
性命之原而剛健中正之懿與之相似而不違
以一身建中和之極而含弘光大之體與之克
肖而無忝其發之也高大光明而高明之德與
天配也其積之也廣博深厚而博厚之德與地
配也上下同流而渾合無間日新之盛德謂不
克配於天地矣乎大生廣生萬物之竝育固至
賾而不可限矣惟天子者裁成天地之道而一
punctuated:
考試官學正宋批〔順暢〕

聖君之合乎造化，於其德業徵之矣。夫德配天地，德之盛也；兼利萬物，業之大也。天子如此，其參於天地也宜哉！經解記孔子之言也，嘗謂天地之大也，夫人難乎其參矣。獨不觀聖人在天子之位乎？是故乾稱乎父，坤稱乎母，而大君則宗子於其間；天位乎上，地位乎下，而聖人則成位於其中。崇效卑法，而神化以備；仰觀俯察，而人極以立。參乎天地者，其惟天子也已矣。蓋嘗自其盛德大業而觀之：今夫大哉至哉，天地之爲德，固極盛而無以加矣。惟天子者，以一心涵性命之原，而剛健中正之懿，與之相似而不違；以一身建中和之極，而含弘光大之體，與之克肖而無忝。其發之也，高大光明，而高明之德與天配也；其積之也，廣博深厚，而博厚之德與地配也。上下同流，而渾合無間，日新之盛德，謂不克配於天地矣乎？大生廣生，萬物之竝育，固至賾而不可限矣。惟天子者，裁成天地之道，而一
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Song, Instructor: 〔Smooth and fluent.〕

The sage ruler’s accord with the creative transformations of nature is attested by his virtue and achievements. That his virtue matches Heaven and Earth shows its fullness; that he benefits all things alike shows the greatness of his achievements. With the Son of Heaven being thus, how fitting that he should stand alongside Heaven and Earth as their third! The “Explanation of the Classics” records these words of Confucius. I have often reflected that, so great are Heaven and Earth, it is difficult for a person to stand alongside them. Yet have we not observed the sage occupying the position of Son of Heaven? Thus Qian is called father and Kun mother, while the great ruler is the principal heir between them. Heaven occupies its place above and Earth its place below, while the sage establishes his place in their midst. He emulates Heaven’s loftiness and models himself on Earth’s lowliness, thereby bringing spiritual transformation to completeness; he looks upward and examines below, thereby establishing the supreme standard for humanity. Surely it is the Son of Heaven alone who stands alongside Heaven and Earth.

Let us consider this through his abundant virtue and great achievements. How great, how consummate is the virtue of Heaven and Earth! Its fullness indeed admits of no addition. The Son of Heaven alone embraces within his single heart the source of human nature and destiny: in the excellence of his strength, vigor, centrality, and correctness, he resembles Heaven without departing from it. In his own person he establishes the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony: in his capacious, comprehensive, luminous, and great substance, he fully resembles Earth without falling short. When his virtue issues forth, it is lofty, great, radiant, and bright; in its loftiness and brightness it matches Heaven. As it accumulates, it is broad, extensive, deep, and substantial; in its breadth and depth it matches Earth. Flowing together with what is above and below, it merges with them into an undivided whole. Can his abundant virtue, renewed each day, be said to fall short of matching Heaven and Earth?

Through Heaven’s mighty generation and Earth’s expansive generation, all things are nourished together: this is indeed supremely intricate and admits of no limit. The Son of Heaven alone regulates and brings to completion the Way of Heaven and Earth, and with a single…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
體之公能使天下無一物不得其所輔相天地
之宜而茂對之心能使天下無一物不被其澤
盡已之性而盡人之性則自夫物之同類者而
利之也盡人之性而盡物之性則自夫物之異
類者而利之也過化存神而曲成不遺富有之
大業謂不兼利夫萬物矣乎夫曰德配天地則
天子與天地同體曰兼利萬物則天子與天地
同用體用備而法象昭信乎可以與天地參矣
抑先儒有云仁者以天地萬物為一體是故天
===
子之參於天地非有所增益於性分之外也夫
亦全乎其所謂一體者而已矣然天地之大也
人猶有所憾惟天子建中和之極而後覆載生
成之偏者得以彌綸而範圍之則雖謂天子之
有功於天地可也故曰天者羣物之祖地者羣
物之母聖人者羣物之命
第貳場
論
萬世文字之祖
punctuated:
體之公，能使天下無一物不得其所；輔相天地之宜，而茂對之心，能使天下無一物不被其澤。盡已之性而盡人之性，則自夫物之同類者而利之也；盡人之性而盡物之性，則自夫物之異類者而利之也。過化存神，而曲成不遺，富有之大業，謂不兼利夫萬物矣乎？夫曰德配天地，則天子與天地同體；曰兼利萬物，則天子與天地同用。體用備而法象昭，信乎可以與天地參矣！抑先儒有云：「仁者以天地萬物為一體。」是故天子之參於天地，非有所增益於性分之外也，夫亦全乎其所謂一體者而已矣。然天地之大也，人猶有所憾。惟天子建中和之極，而後覆載生成之偏者，得以彌綸而範圍之，則雖謂天子之有功於天地可也。故曰：「天者，羣物之祖；地者，羣物之母；聖人者，羣物之命。」
第貳場
論
萬世文字之祖
translation_en:
…the impartiality of forming one body with all things enables him to ensure that nothing under Heaven fails to find its proper place. By assisting Heaven and Earth in what is fitting, his resolve to respond fully to them ensures that nothing under Heaven goes untouched by his beneficence. By fully realizing his own nature and thereby fully realizing the nature of others, he benefits those beings that belong to his own kind; by fully realizing the nature of others and thereby fully realizing the nature of things, he benefits those beings that belong to different kinds. Wherever he passes, transformation follows; wherever he abides, his influence is spiritual. He brings each thing to fulfillment according to its particular circumstances, leaving none out. Can this great undertaking, so rich in its possessions, be said not to benefit all things alike? To say that his virtue matches Heaven and Earth means that the Son of Heaven shares their substance; to say that he benefits all things alike means that he shares their functioning. With substance and functioning both complete, and their exemplary patterns manifest, he can indeed stand as a third alongside Heaven and Earth!
Moreover, an earlier Confucian scholar said: “The benevolent person forms one body with Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things.” Thus, the Son of Heaven’s standing as a third alongside Heaven and Earth adds nothing beyond what is inherent in his nature. He merely brings to completeness what is meant by forming one body with them. Yet, great as Heaven and Earth are, people still find cause for regret. Only when the Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony can the unevenness in their sheltering, supporting, generating, and nurturing be comprehensively ordered and brought within proper bounds. Thus, one may even say that the Son of Heaven renders service to Heaven and Earth. Hence it is said: “Heaven is the progenitor of all things; Earth is the mother of all things; the sage is the life of all things.”
Second Session
Discourse
The Progenitor of Writing for All Ages

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
王弘誨
同考試官教諭蕭批論場不知易者每至空
疎固陋而知者又復散漫支離惟此篇融會先天
之圖深於理數而復文勢沛然若江河之決而莫
之禦是宜錄出
同考試官教諭曾批萬世文字之祖人多知
出陳氏而不知為朱子之論司馬遷此作考據精
詳而步驟縱逸抑揚開闔俱有程度真佳作也可
以式矣
===
考試官教諭黃批詞宏氣昌大家氣象
考試官學正宋批雄健之作
道之大原出於天也聖人承天心以闡道而人
文於是乎啓矣作易非聖人意也天也太極動
而陽生焉靜而陰生焉動靜互為其根而循環
無窮焉此天之道也天不能自秘其道而於圖
乎見之聖人者發天地之蘊通神明之德而援
此以立象而先天之圖畫焉蓋先天地而知天
地之終後天地而知天地之始惟以闡道也而
punctuated:
王弘誨

同考試官教諭蕭批：論場不知易者，每至空疎固陋，而知者又復散漫支離。惟此篇融會先天之圖，深於理數，而復文勢沛然，若江河之決而莫之禦，是宜錄出。

同考試官教諭曾批：萬世文字之祖，人多知出陳氏，而不知為朱子之論司馬遷。此作考據精詳，而步驟縱逸，抑揚開闔俱有程度，真佳作也，可以式矣。

考試官教諭黃批：詞宏氣昌，大家氣象。

考試官學正宋批：雄健之作。

道之大原出於天也。聖人承天心以闡道，而人文於是乎啓矣。作易非聖人意也，天也。太極動而陽生焉，靜而陰生焉，動靜互為其根而循環無窮焉，此天之道也。天不能自秘其道，而於圖乎見之。聖人者，發天地之蘊，通神明之德，而援此以立象，而先天之圖畫焉。蓋先天地而知天地之終，後天地而知天地之始，惟以闡道也，而
translation_en:
Wang Honghui 王弘誨

Comment by Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor: In the discourse session, those who do not understand the Book of Changes frequently lapse into empty, shallow, and narrow treatments, while those who do understand it nevertheless become diffuse and disjointed. This essay alone integrates the Diagram of the Prior Heaven, displaying a profound grasp of principle and number. Its prose also surges forward like great rivers bursting their banks, which nothing can restrain. It deserves to be selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zeng, Instructor: Most people know that “the progenitor of writing for all ages” comes from Master Chen, but do not know that it was Zhu Xi’s assessment of Sima Qian. This composition is precise and thorough in its examination of sources, yet free and untrammeled in its progression. Its rises and falls, openings and closings, all observe due measure. It is truly an excellent composition and may serve as a model.

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: Grand diction and abundant vigor—the bearing of a great master.

Comment by Examiner Song, School Instructor: A powerful and vigorous composition.

The great source of the Way comes from Heaven. The sages received Heaven’s intent and elucidated the Way; human culture thus began. The making of the Book of Changes arose not from the sages’ intention, but from Heaven. When the Supreme Ultimate moves, yang is generated; when it is still, yin is generated. Movement and stillness each serve as the root of the other, cycling without end: this is the Way of Heaven. Heaven could not keep its Way concealed, but manifested it in a diagram. The sages revealed what lay hidden within Heaven and Earth and comprehended the powers of the spirits. Drawing upon this, they established the images, and thus the Diagram of the Prior Heaven was drawn. Before Heaven and Earth, they knew the end of Heaven and Earth; after Heaven and Earth, they knew the beginning of Heaven and Earth. Their sole purpose was to elucidate the Way, and …

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
非以爲文也而天下後世之文卒不能外焉天
地之紀典則之會萬事萬化之原胥於是乎出
是豈聖人有所强於天下後世哉聖人無所强
於天下後世而道之所在天下後世不得不從
天下後世未始求文於聖人而文之所在天下
後世不得不祖非祖其文也祖其道也非祖聖
人之道祖天之道也大矣哉先天之易也茲其
爲萬世文字之祖乎今夫鴻濛之世顓侗沕穆
雖有畫前之易與天下相忘於無言之天聖人
===
之所樂也逮伏羲氏作而先天之圖畫焉聖人
豈故爲是贅哉風氣日開人文漸著造化之精
天亦不能自秘而河圖於是乎出焉一六居下
二七居上三八居左四九居右五十居中此自
然之數也天之文亦天之道也然是圖也夫人
而皆見之不夫人而皆知之伏羲氏之王天下
也首出庶物因天開人於是神道設教而卦畫
焉虛五與十而太極之體立矣積二十之奇合
二十之偶以一二三四合七八九六而儀象定
punctuated:
非以爲文也，而天下後世之文卒不能外焉。天地之紀，典則之會，萬事萬化之原，胥於是乎出。是豈聖人有所强於天下後世哉？聖人無所强於天下後世，而道之所在，天下後世不得不從；天下後世未始求文於聖人，而文之所在，天下後世不得不祖。非祖其文也，祖其道也；非祖聖人之道，祖天之道也。大矣哉，先天之易也！茲其爲萬世文字之祖乎！
今夫鴻濛之世，顓侗沕穆，雖有畫前之易，與天下相忘於無言之天，聖人之所樂也。逮伏羲氏作，而先天之圖畫焉。聖人豈故爲是贅哉？風氣日開，人文漸著，造化之精，天亦不能自秘，而河圖於是乎出焉。一六居下，二七居上，三八居左，四九居右，五十居中，此自然之數也。天之文，亦天之道也。然是圖也，夫人而皆見之，不夫人而皆知之。伏羲氏之王天下也，首出庶物，因天開人，於是神道設教，而卦畫焉。虛五與十，而太極之體立矣；積二十之奇，合二十之偶，以一二三四合七八九六，而儀象定
translation_en:
…not for the purpose of creating literary forms; yet the writings of all later ages ultimately could not go beyond them. The ordering principles of Heaven and Earth, the convergence of norms and standards, and the source of all affairs and transformations all issue from this. Did the sage impose anything upon the world and later generations? The sage imposed nothing upon them; yet where the Way resides, the world and later generations cannot but follow. The world and later generations never sought literary forms from the sage; yet where those forms reside, they cannot but take them as their model. They model themselves not on his literary forms but on his Way—not on the sage’s Way, but on Heaven’s Way. Great indeed is the Earlier Heaven Book of Changes! Surely it is the ancestor of the writings of all ages!
Now, in the age of primordial chaos, all was simple, undifferentiated, profound, and still. Although the Changes already existed before the drawing of the trigrams, the sage and the world forgot one another within a Heaven without words: this was what the sage delighted in. When Fuxi arose, the Earlier Heaven Diagram was drawn. Could the sage deliberately have made such a superfluous addition? As the tendencies of the age unfolded day by day and human culture gradually became manifest, even Heaven could no longer keep the essence of creation concealed; thus the River Chart appeared. One and six occupy the bottom, two and seven the top, three and eight the left, four and nine the right, and five and ten the center. These are the numbers of the natural order. Heaven’s pattern is also Heaven’s Way. Yet although everyone could see this chart, not everyone could understand it. When Fuxi ruled the world, he stood foremost among all beings and, following Heaven, enlightened humanity. Thus he established instruction through the numinous Way, and the trigrams were drawn. By leaving five and ten vacant, the structure of the Supreme Ultimate was established. By accumulating the odd numbers totaling twenty and combining the even numbers totaling twenty, and by joining one, two, three, and four with seven, eight, nine, and six, the two modes and four images were determined…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
矣折四方之合補四隅之空而八卦位矣是豈
聖人勉强矯拂於其間哉一因其數之自然而
不可易道之本然而不可容强者耳自今觀之
圖之從中起也易之本太極也是卽萬事萬化
生於心也乾健坤順也艮止震動也離麗而兌
說也坎陷而巽入也卽吾心性情之德也萬之
原於一也奇者陽之文也偶者陰之文也奇奇
偶偶者象之文也三畫皆奇乾之文也三畫皆
偶坤之文也以至奇偶之或上或下或多或寡
===
則震巽坎離艮兌之文也因而重之則自復至
乾自姤至坤六十四卦之文也縱横錯綜莫不
各有其理對待流行莫不各有其義而天下之
文昭矣蓋自本而幹自幹而枝若有所迫而自
不能已何莫而非自然之數自然之道耶由是
聖人發揮於辭而筆之經無不可者何止于圖
而靳於言耶噫聖人之精因畫以示使天下後
世有因畫而求吾心焉則文固燦然而具陳道
固渾然而具在如以畫而已矣則盈天地間皆
punctuated:
矣。折四方之合，補四隅之空，而八卦位矣。是豈聖人勉强矯拂於其間哉？一因其數之自然而不可易、道之本然而不可容强者耳。自今觀之，圖之從中起也，易之本太極也，是卽萬事萬化生於心也。乾健坤順也，艮止震動也，離麗而兌說也，坎陷而巽入也，卽吾心性情之德也。萬之原於一也，奇者陽之文也，偶者陰之文也，奇奇偶偶者象之文也。三畫皆奇，乾之文也；三畫皆偶，坤之文也。以至奇偶之或上或下、或多或寡，則震巽坎離艮兌之文也。因而重之，則自復至乾、自姤至坤，六十四卦之文也。縱横錯綜，莫不各有其理；對待流行，莫不各有其義，而天下之文昭矣。蓋自本而幹，自幹而枝，若有所迫而自不能已，何莫而非自然之數、自然之道耶？由是聖人發揮於辭而筆之經，無不可者，何止于圖而靳於言耶？
噫！聖人之精，因畫以示，使天下後世有因畫而求吾心焉，則文固燦然而具陳，道固渾然而具在。如以畫而已矣，則盈天地間皆
translation_en:
…are established. By dividing the combinations at the four sides and filling the empty spaces at the four corners, the eight trigrams are assigned their positions. Could this be a matter of the sage forcibly intervening and bending things against their nature? He simply follows the natural, unalterable character of the numbers and the inherent character of the Way, which admits no coercion. Viewed from the present, the diagram’s beginning at its center and the Changes’ grounding in the Supreme Ultimate signify precisely that the myriad affairs and transformations arise from the heart-mind. Qian is vigorous and Kun yielding; Gen is still and Zhen moving; Li is clinging and Dui joyous; Kan is sinking into a pit and Xun entering. These are precisely the qualities of the nature and feelings of our heart-minds.
The myriad originate in the one. Odd numbers are the pattern of yang; even numbers are the pattern of yin; combinations of odd and even are the patterns of the images. Three lines all odd form the pattern of Qian; three lines all even form the pattern of Kun. When odd and even occupy upper or lower positions, or are more or fewer in number, they form the patterns of Zhen, Xun, Kan, Li, Gen, and Dui. Doubling these produces the patterns of the sixty-four hexagrams, from Fu to Qian and from Gou to Kun. Arranged vertically and horizontally, interlaced and combined, each has its principle; in opposition and in flowing succession, each has its significance. Thus the patterns of all under Heaven become manifest. From root to trunk, and from trunk to branches, they seem impelled by something and unable to stop of themselves. Which of these is not natural number and the natural Way? Accordingly, there is nothing inappropriate in the sage’s elaborating them in verbal statements and committing them to writing in the classic. Why should he stop at the diagram and be sparing with words?
Ah! The sage reveals his essential understanding through the lines, so that people throughout the world in later generations may follow the lines and seek it within their own heart-minds. The patterns are indeed brilliantly displayed in their entirety, and the Way is indeed wholly present as an undivided whole. If one takes them to be merely lines, then everything filling the space between Heaven and Earth is…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
神化之糟粕耳此則聖人意也然雖無文也而
天下之至文存焉無言也而天下之至言在焉
聖人非有求於天下萬世而其文其道自有以
通乎天下萬世之人心天下萬世非有期於聖
人而不能不取足於聖人之文之道是故黃帝
堯舜得之而爲垂衣之治湯武得之而爲順應
之舉文王箕子得之而爲艱貞之行莫非此道
也莫非此文之祖也夏后氏之連山商人之歸
藏文王之彖辭周公之爻辭孔子之十翼莫非
===
此道也莫非此文之祖也以動者尚其變以言
者尚其辭以制器者尚其象以卜筮者尚其占
莫非此道也莫非此文之祖也溫柔敦厚之詩
疏通知遠之書恭敬退讓之禮廣博易良之樂
屬辭比事之春秋莫非此道也莫非此文之祖
也以至萬事萬化稼穡耒耜舟車宮室書契臼
杵弧矢市易以開天下之物以成天下之務何
莫而非此道何莫而非此文之祖耶是非聖人
之意之也先天無言之秘實有以闡三才之理
punctuated: 神化之糟粕耳，此則聖人意也。然雖無文也，而天下之至文存焉；無言也，而天下之至言在焉。聖人非有求於天下萬世，而其文其道自有以通乎天下萬世之人心；天下萬世非有期於聖人，而不能不取足於聖人之文之道。是故黃帝、堯、舜得之，而爲垂衣之治；湯、武得之，而爲順應之舉；文王、箕子得之，而爲艱貞之行。莫非此道也，莫非此文之祖也。夏后氏之《連山》、商人之《歸藏》、文王之彖辭、周公之爻辭、孔子之《十翼》，莫非此道也，莫非此文之祖也。以動者尚其變，以言者尚其辭，以制器者尚其象，以卜筮者尚其占，莫非此道也，莫非此文之祖也。溫柔敦厚之《詩》、疏通知遠之《書》、恭敬退讓之《禮》、廣博易良之《樂》、屬辭比事之《春秋》，莫非此道也，莫非此文之祖也。以至萬事萬化，稼穡、耒耜、舟車、宮室、書契、臼杵、弧矢、市易，以開天下之物，以成天下之務，何莫而非此道，何莫而非此文之祖耶？是非聖人之意之也？先天無言之秘，實有以闡三才之理
translation_en:
…merely the dregs of numinous transformation. This, then, is the sage’s intention. Yet although there is no writing, the supreme pattern of all under Heaven subsists therein; although there are no words, the supreme utterance of all under Heaven is present therein. The sage seeks nothing from the world through all ages, yet his pattern and his Way naturally have the means to reach the hearts of people throughout the world and through all ages. The world through all ages expects nothing of the sage, yet cannot help finding all it needs in his pattern and his Way. Thus Huangdi, Yao, and Shun attained it and achieved government by merely letting their robes hang down; Tang and Wu attained it and undertook actions in accordance with Heaven and in response to the people; King Wen and Jizi attained it and practiced steadfastness amid hardship. All these embody this Way; all are sources of this pattern.

The Linked Mountains (Lianshan) of the Xia rulers, the Return to the Hidden (Guicang) of the Shang people, King Wen’s judgments on the hexagrams, the Duke of Zhou’s statements on the lines, and Confucius’s Ten Wings all embody this Way; all are sources of this pattern. Those who act prize its changes; those who speak prize its statements; those who make implements prize its images; those who divine by turtle shell and milfoil prize its prognostications. All these embody this Way; all are sources of this pattern. The Poetry, with its gentleness, sincerity, and generosity; the Documents, with its breadth of understanding and knowledge of distant times; the Rites, with its reverence and deference; the Music, with its breadth, ease, and goodness; and the Spring and Autumn Annals, with its arrangement of words and juxtaposition of events—all embody this Way; all are sources of this pattern.

Extending even to the myriad affairs and transformations—to sowing and reaping, plows and plowshares, boats and carriages, palaces and dwellings, written records and tallies, mortars and pestles, bows and arrows, and market exchange—these develop the things of the world and bring its affairs to completion. Which of them does not embody this Way? Which of them is not a source of this pattern? Is this not the sage’s intention [?]? The wordless mystery of the Prior-to-Heaven arrangement truly has the means to elucidate the principles of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
則立極垂憲一無言之圖而固有以冒天下之
道矣由是千百世之下有聖人出焉非祖其文
祖其道非祖聖人之道天不變則道亦不變自
有以範圍而不過焉耳易不云乎聖人立象以
盡意知象之可以盡意則知圖之可以盡文矣
又云天生神物聖人則之則圖之原於天而不
可易不亦彰彰著明矣哉夫先天之圖爲萬世
文字之祖史遷紀五帝而顧獨遺焉陋矣宜子
朱子之所爲興慨也若之何後之言易者紛紛
===
也有五行有卦氣有太玄有洞極有潛虚其不
知所祖而昧焉者乎有圖說有通書有易傳有
啟蒙有皇極經世其知所祖而明焉者乎夫先
天之學多言以晦之固易之障也而得諸儒以
爲之羽翼而大明又易之幸也哉
同前
何天衢
同考試官敎諭童 批
卦畫所以爲文字之祖
處模寫殆盡非潛心易學者未易到此佳士佳士
punctuated:
則立極垂憲，一無言之圖，而固有以冒天下之道矣。由是千百世之下，有聖人出焉，非祖其文，祖其道；非祖聖人之道，天不變則道亦不變，自有以範圍而不過焉耳。《易》不云乎：「聖人立象以盡意。」知象之可以盡意，則知圖之可以盡文矣。又云：「天生神物，聖人則之。」則圖之原於天而不可易，不亦彰彰著明矣哉！夫先天之圖爲萬世文字之祖，史遷紀五帝，而顧獨遺焉，陋矣！宜子朱子之所爲興慨也。若之何後之言《易》者紛紛也？有五行，有卦氣，有《太玄》，有《洞極》，有《潛虚》，其不知所祖而昧焉者乎？有《圖說》，有《通書》，有《易傳》，有《啟蒙》，有《皇極經世》，其知所祖而明焉者乎？夫先天之學，多言以晦之，固《易》之障也；而得諸儒以爲之羽翼而大明，又《易》之幸也哉！

同前
何天衢

同考試官敎諭童批：「卦畫所以爲文字之祖處，模寫殆盡。非潛心易學者，未易到此。佳士！佳士！」
translation_en:
…thus establishing the ultimate standard and bequeathing a lasting model: a single wordless diagram indeed encompasses the Way of all under Heaven. Hence, if a sage should arise a thousand or a hundred generations later, he would take as his model not its writing but its Way—not merely the Way of the sages, for as Heaven does not change, neither does the Way. It inherently encompasses everything without overstepping its bounds. Does not the Book of Changes say, “The sages established images to express their meaning fully”? Knowing that images can fully express meaning, we know that the diagram can fully express all that writing conveys. It also says, “Heaven produces numinous things, and the sages take them as models.” Is it not therefore abundantly clear that the diagram originates in Heaven and cannot be altered? The Diagram of the Before-Heaven Arrangement is the progenitor of writing for all ages, yet the historian Sima Qian, in recording the Five Emperors, omitted this alone. How limited his understanding! No wonder Master Zhu Xi lamented it. Why, then, have later interpreters of the Changes produced such a profusion of divergent accounts? There are the Five Phases, the theory of hexagram qi, the Supreme Mystery (Taixuan), Penetrating the Ultimate (Dongji), and Latent Emptiness (Qianxu). Are these not instances of obscurity through ignorance of their proper source? There are the Explanation of the Diagram (Tushuo), the Comprehensive Writings (Tongshu), the Commentary on the Changes (Yizhuan), the Introduction to Learning (Qimeng), and the Supreme Principle for Ordering the World (Huangji jingshi). Are these not instances of clarity through knowledge of their proper source? To obscure the learning of the Before-Heaven Arrangement with excessive words is indeed an impediment to understanding the Changes. Yet that these Confucian scholars should have lent it their support and made it brilliantly clear—what good fortune for the Changes!

Same topic as the preceding essay.
He Tianqu.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tong, Instructor: “The point concerning how the hexagram lines became the progenitor of writing is expounded almost exhaustively. Someone who had not devoted himself wholeheartedly to the study of the Changes could scarcely attain this level. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!”

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭孫批詞格高古氣象宏大開
闔變化意趣不窮亦文字之有數者錄之
考試官教諭黃批有源委有波瀾
考試官學正宋批氣槩闊大
天有顯道也聖人作易以開斯道之原其達諸
天乎夫天者道之原也天不言而以道示人夫
人囿于斯道日用而不知也不能不賴聖人以
開其原聖人者天之所命首出庶物神靈特異
先天地而知天地之終後天地而知天地之始
===
承天之意而作易以開斯道之原使天下後世
緣其原而得其所以達諸天者斯文賴以著明
謂非聖人立道之極而爲吾道之祖不可也孔
子傳易而首包犧曰包犧氏始作作者創之謂
也後有作者述之而已矣知乎此則伏羲作易而
爲萬世文字之祖者可得而論矣爰自混沌未
鑿鴻濛未闢一元之氣渾淪而已矣固無所謂
道也迨夫天開於子而爲羣物之祖地闢於丑
而爲羣物之母人生於寅而聖人成位乎中故
punctuated:
同考試官教諭孫批：詞格高古，氣象宏大，開闔變化，意趣不窮，亦文字之有數者，錄之。
考試官教諭黃批：有源委，有波瀾。
考試官學正宋批：氣槩闊大。
天有顯道也，聖人作易以開斯道之原，其達諸天乎？夫天者，道之原也。天不言，而以道示人。夫人囿于斯道，日用而不知也，不能不賴聖人以開其原。聖人者，天之所命，首出庶物，神靈特異，先天地而知天地之終，後天地而知天地之始，承天之意而作易，以開斯道之原，使天下後世緣其原而得其所以達諸天者，斯文賴以著明。謂非聖人立道之極而爲吾道之祖，不可也。孔子傳易而首包犧，曰：「包犧氏始作。」作者，創之謂也。後有作者，述之而已矣。知乎此，則伏羲作易而爲萬世文字之祖者，可得而論矣。爰自混沌未鑿，鴻濛未闢，一元之氣渾淪而已矣，固無所謂道也。迨夫天開於子而爲羣物之祖，地闢於丑而爲羣物之母，人生於寅而聖人成位乎中，故
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Instructor: The diction and style are lofty and antique, and the overall bearing is grand. Its unfolding and closing, its shifts and transformations, offer inexhaustible meaning and interest. This too ranks among the outstanding compositions [?]. Include it.
Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: It has a source and a course, and waves and surges.
Comment by Examiner Song, School Instructor: Its spirit is expansive and grand.
Heaven has a manifest Way. The sage composed the Book of Changes to disclose the source of this Way: did he thereby attain communion with Heaven? Heaven is the source of the Way. Heaven does not speak, but shows the Way to humankind. People live within this Way and use it daily without knowing it; they therefore cannot but depend upon the sage to disclose its source. The sage is commissioned by Heaven, standing foremost among all beings, possessed of uniquely wondrous spiritual powers. Preceding Heaven and Earth, he knows their end; following Heaven and Earth, he knows their beginning. He received Heaven’s intent and composed the Book of Changes to disclose the source of this Way, enabling all under Heaven and later generations to follow its source and discover the means of attaining communion with Heaven. Through this, our cultural tradition was made manifest. One cannot deny that the sage established the ultimate standard of the Way and became the progenitor of our Way. In transmitting the Book of Changes, Confucius placed Baoxi first, saying, “Baoxi first created it.” To create means to originate something. Those who came afterward as creators merely transmitted it. Once this is understood, we may discuss how Fuxi, by composing the Book of Changes, became the progenitor of writing for all ages. At the outset, before primordial chaos had been hewn open and the primeval vastness had been divided, there was only the undifferentiated vital force of the primal unity. There was as yet nothing that could be called the Way. Then Heaven opened in the zi phase and became the progenitor of all beings; Earth opened in the chou phase and became their mother; humankind arose in the yin phase, and the sage took his proper place between them. Thus …

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
聖人者天地之宗子民物之祖也三皇之時風
氣未開太朴未琢民生其間與草木鹿豕何異
巢窟可居未有宮室之文羽毛可蔽未有冠裳
之文男女無别未有嫁娶之文結繩而治未有
書契之文斯時也道固未彰也及夫包犧氏作
以木德王天下天地之盛德在木帝出乎震包
犧氏應運而興時則於氣爲泰於令爲春故曰
其帝太昊蓋又天地一大開闢也是故華渚流
虹明象日月而聖德徵矣天應以鳥獸文章地
===
應以河圖洛書而貞符協矣伏羲氏亦烏能如
渾敦之時與斯世相忘於沕穆之天哉夫龍馬
負圖而出也固天所以示文明之精而洩斯道
之原也伏羲仰觀俯察遠求近取則其圖稽其
數由太極而兩儀由兩儀而四象由四象而八
卦剛柔以立其本動靜以互其根是故其體微
而彰其事閎而肆其理約而精聖人者由此而
發揮於詞模寫於經可也包犧氏何靳於言而
不與天下萬世立教哉噫聖人非不言也聖人
punctuated: 聖人者，天地之宗子，民物之祖也。三皇之時，風氣未開，太朴未琢，民生其間，與草木鹿豕何異？巢窟可居，未有宮室之文；羽毛可蔽，未有冠裳之文；男女無别，未有嫁娶之文；結繩而治，未有書契之文。斯時也，道固未彰也。及夫包犧氏作，以木德王天下，天地之盛德在木，帝出乎震。包犧氏應運而興，時則於氣爲泰，於令爲春，故曰其帝太昊。蓋又天地一大開闢也。是故華渚流虹，明象日月，而聖德徵矣；天應以鳥獸文章，地應以河圖洛書，而貞符協矣。伏羲氏亦烏能如渾敦之時，與斯世相忘於沕穆之天哉？夫龍馬負圖而出也，固天所以示文明之精而洩斯道之原也。伏羲仰觀俯察，遠求近取，則其圖，稽其數，由太極而兩儀，由兩儀而四象，由四象而八卦。剛柔以立其本，動靜以互其根。是故其體微而彰，其事閎而肆，其理約而精。聖人者，由此而發揮於詞，模寫於經，可也。包犧氏何靳於言，而不與天下萬世立教哉？噫！聖人非不言也，聖人
translation_en:
…the sage is the principal heir of Heaven and Earth and the progenitor of the people and all beings. In the age of the Three Sovereigns, civilizing influences had yet to unfold, and primal simplicity remained uncarved. How were the people living then different from plants and trees, deer and swine? Nests and caves provided dwellings, but there was as yet no cultured form of palaces and houses; feathers and pelts provided coverings, but there was no cultured form of caps and robes. Men and women were undifferentiated, and there were no marriage rites; government was conducted through knotted cords, and there were no written documents. At that time, the Way had certainly not yet become manifest.

When Baoxi arose, he ruled All-under-Heaven through the virtue of Wood. The flourishing virtue of Heaven and Earth lay in Wood: “The Sovereign comes forth in Zhen.” Baoxi arose in response to the destined cycle. In its vital energies, the time corresponded to Tai, harmonious concord; in its seasonal order, to spring. Hence the saying, “Its sovereign is Taihao.” This was yet another great opening of Heaven and Earth. Thus a rainbow streamed at Huazhu, and brightness imaged the sun and moon [?], revealing signs of sagely virtue. Heaven responded with the patterned markings of birds and beasts, and Earth responded with the Yellow River Chart and the Luo River Writing: the auspicious tokens accorded. How could Fuxi, as in the age of primordial chaos, remain oblivious to the world, and the world to him, beneath a heaven of deep tranquillity?

The dragon-horse emerged bearing the Chart: this was precisely how Heaven displayed the essence of civilization and disclosed the source of this Way. Fuxi looked upward and observed, looked downward and examined, sought afar and drew upon what was near. He took the Chart as his model and investigated its numbers: from the Supreme Ultimate came the Two Modes; from the Two Modes, the Four Images; and from the Four Images, the Eight Trigrams. The firm and the yielding established their foundation; movement and stillness served as each other’s root. Thus their structure was subtle yet manifest, their scope vast and far-reaching, and their principles concise and refined. From this, the sage could have elaborated his meaning in words and set it down in a classic. Why, then, was Baoxi sparing with words, rather than establishing a teaching for All-under-Heaven through all ages? Ah! It was not that the sage did not speak. The sage…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之意以為吾示以畫使天下後世緣畫而求諸
心焉則得意忘象得象忘言盈天地間糟粕煨
燼固無非教也徒以畫而已則圖書不過象數
之迹雖言焉亦贅疣矣噫此聖人待天下意也
自今觀之一奇一偶者儀之文也奇偶各二者
象之文也奇偶之純乾坤之文也奇偶之雜則
震巽坎離艮兌之文也因而重之則六十四卦
之文昭矣斯不亦微而彰乎日月星辰水火土
石剛柔之體用也寒暑晝夜風雨露雷陰陽之
===
消息也性情形體飛走草木象形之變動也斯
不亦閎而肆乎虛五與十而為太極所以具吾
心之體也健順動止麗說陷入所以達性情之
用也神明之德通焉性命之理寓焉斯不亦約
而精乎噫此圖之所以至妙至妙也無文也而
實萬世之至文無言也而實萬世之至言道不
在茲乎後有作者堯舜紹之而作十六字湯武
承之而作誓誥文王衍之而作卦辭周公係爻
孔子著傳蓋統於六經而文字始盛矣至於孟
punctuated: 之意以為：吾示以畫，使天下後世緣畫而求諸心焉，則得意忘象，得象忘言，盈天地間糟粕煨燼，固無非教也。徒以畫而已，則圖書不過象數之迹，雖言焉，亦贅疣矣。噫！此聖人待天下意也。自今觀之，一奇一偶者，儀之文也；奇偶各二者，象之文也；奇偶之純，乾坤之文也；奇偶之雜，則震巽坎離艮兌之文也。因而重之，則六十四卦之文昭矣。斯不亦微而彰乎？日月星辰，水火土石，剛柔之體用也；寒暑晝夜，風雨露雷，陰陽之消息也；性情形體，飛走草木，象形之變動也。斯不亦閎而肆乎？虛五與十而為太極，所以具吾心之體也；健順動止，麗說陷入，所以達性情之用也。神明之德通焉，性命之理寓焉。斯不亦約而精乎？噫！此圖之所以至妙至妙也。無文也，而實萬世之至文；無言也，而實萬世之至言。道不在茲乎？後有作者，堯舜紹之而作十六字，湯武承之而作誓誥，文王衍之而作卦辭，周公係爻，孔子著傳，蓋統於六經而文字始盛矣。至於孟
translation_en: …his intention was this: “I show them through drawn lines, so that all under Heaven and later generations may follow those lines and seek within their own hearts. Then, grasping the meaning, they may forget the images; grasping the images, they may forget the words. Even the dregs and ashes that fill Heaven and Earth are surely all teaching. If they concern themselves only with the drawn lines, however, the River Chart and Luo Writing are merely traces of images and numbers; even if words were supplied, they would be superfluous excrescences.” Ah! Such was the sage’s intention toward all under Heaven. Viewed from our own time, one odd and one even line constitute the pattern of the Two Modes; combinations of two odd or even lines constitute the patterns of the Four Images. Pure odd or pure even lines constitute the patterns of Qian and Kun; mixtures of odd and even constitute the patterns of Zhen, Xun, Kan, Li, Gen, and Dui. By doubling these, the patterns of the sixty-four hexagrams become manifest. Is this not subtle yet apparent? Sun, moon, stars, and constellations; water, fire, earth, and stone: these are the substance and functioning of the firm and yielding. Cold and heat, day and night, wind, rain, dew, and thunder: these are the waning and waxing of yin and yang. Nature and feelings, forms and bodies, flying and running creatures, grasses and trees: these are the transformations and movements of images and forms. Is this not vast and far-reaching? Setting aside five and ten to constitute the Supreme Ultimate provides the full substance of our hearts. Strength, compliance, movement, stillness, attachment, joy, peril, and entry give expression to the functioning of our nature and feelings. Through these, the potency of spiritual illumination flows, and within them reside the principles of human nature and destiny. Is this not concise and refined? Ah! This is why the Chart is supremely, supremely wondrous. It has no writing, yet is truly the supreme writing for all ages; it has no words, yet is truly the supreme utterance for all ages. Does not the Way reside here? Later there arose those who composed writings: Yao and Shun continued this legacy and composed the sixteen characters; Tang and Wu inherited it and composed oaths and proclamations; King Wen developed it and composed the hexagram statements; the Duke of Zhou appended the line statements; and Kongzi wrote the commentaries. These were gathered within the Six Classics, and written expression then began to flourish. As for Meng…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
子七篇而文字始辨矣然何莫而非祖於圖哉
蓋數聖人者冥會於異世之感神明其得意之
象所以作之於經垂之於訓凡言乎陰陽者體
其微而彰者也言乎天地萬物者發其閎而肆
者也言乎人心性情者闡其約而精者也不求
之詞而求之畫不求之畫而求之心真可以上
接包犧氏之統而得文字正脉之傳也故論文
字而始於八卦祖伏羲也精於十六字宗堯舜
禹也盛於六經子湯文周孔也辨於七篇孫孟
===
軻也至於諸子百家非無作者不過文字之餘
裔謂其有得於祖述不可也傳易者曰書不盡
言言不盡意聖人立象以盡意知象之可以盡
意則知圖之可以盡文字矣說經者曰易為五
經之原蓋五經皆祖於易而易則祖於畫知易
為五經之祖則圖為文字之祖又可知矣然則
聖人之立卦也果在於文字之間乎蓋聖人之
道達諸天者也天不言而二曜循環列宿經緯
四維奠位莫非文也莫非道也二氣之推遷五
punctuated: 子七篇，而文字始辨矣。然何莫而非祖於圖哉？蓋數聖人者，冥會於異世之感，神明其得意之象，所以作之於經，垂之於訓。凡言乎陰陽者，體其微而彰者也；言乎天地萬物者，發其閎而肆者也；言乎人心性情者，闡其約而精者也。不求之詞而求之畫，不求之畫而求之心，真可以上接包犧氏之統，而得文字正脉之傳也。故論文字而始於八卦，祖伏羲也；精於十六字，宗堯舜禹也；盛於六經，子湯文周孔也；辨於七篇，孫孟軻也。至於諸子百家，非無作者，不過文字之餘裔，謂其有得於祖述，不可也。傳易者曰：「書不盡言，言不盡意。聖人立象以盡意。」知象之可以盡意，則知圖之可以盡文字矣。說經者曰：「易為五經之原。」蓋五經皆祖於易，而易則祖於畫。知易為五經之祖，則圖為文字之祖，又可知矣。然則聖人之立卦也，果在於文字之間乎？蓋聖人之道，達諸天者也。天不言，而二曜循環，列宿經緯，四維奠位，莫非文也，莫非道也。二氣之推遷，五
translation_en:
…with the seven books of Mencius, writing began to acquire discriminating clarity. Yet what among these did not have its origin in the Diagram? These sages met inwardly through a resonance across different ages, bringing spiritual illumination to the images through which they apprehended meaning; thus they embodied it in the classics and handed it down in their teachings. Whatever speaks of yin and yang gives substance to what is subtle yet manifest in the Diagram; whatever speaks of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things unfolds its breadth and expansiveness; whatever speaks of the human mind, nature, and feelings elucidates its concision and refinement. Seek it not in words but in the drawn lines; seek it not in the drawn lines but in the mind. Then one can truly reach back to continue the lineage of Baoxi and receive the transmission of the authentic tradition of writing. Thus, in discussing writing, to locate its beginning in the Eight Trigrams is to take Fuxi as its progenitor; to locate its refinement in the sixteen characters is to revere Yao, Shun, and Yu as its ancestral masters; to locate its flourishing in the Six Classics is to regard Tang, King Wen, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius as its sons; and to locate its discriminating clarity in the seven books is to regard Meng Ke as its grandson. As for the various masters and hundred schools, they certainly had their authors, but these were merely distant descendants of writing. One cannot say that they had grasped how to carry forward the ancestral tradition.

The commentator on the Changes says: “Writing does not exhaust words; words do not exhaust meaning. The sages established images to exhaust meaning.” Once we understand that images can fully express meaning, we understand that the Diagram can encompass all writing. An expositor of the classics says: “The Changes is the source of the Five Classics.” The Five Classics all derive from the Changes, while the Changes derives from the drawn lines. Knowing that the Changes is the progenitor of the Five Classics, we can also understand that the Diagram is the progenitor of writing. Was the sages’ establishment of the trigrams, then, really confined within writing? The Way of the sages reaches through to Heaven. Heaven does not speak, yet the two luminaries revolve, the constellations form their warp and weft, and the four corners occupy their settled positions: all are pattern, and all are the Way. The shifting succession of the two vital forces, the five…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
行之順布以至品物之流形莫非文也莫非道
也聖人法天以作易則圖位布列爻象交錯寧
非所以成天地之文而呈斯道之體哉故天者
道之祖也畫者文之祖也聖人者萬世之祖也
由此而書契易焉甲曆著焉嫁娶辨焉衣裳制
焉宮室作焉朴野變焉文教興焉由此而口代
天言焉手代天工焉心代天意焉身代天事焉
故謂聖人建天下萬世之極可也謂聖人裁成
輔相以左右民亦可也前乎此者三皇莫神焉
===
史稱其澹泊無爲造化之眞宰未彰陰陽之氣
方孕而未育也後乎此者堯舜莫盛焉史稱其
放勳重華造化之元神已暢陰陽之氣長養而
蕃廡也包犧氏上繼三皇應運而生下開羣聖
撫運而治故稱乎祖焉是以論帝系者以包犧
爲五帝之首著月令者以太昊爲四時之春序
書言三墳而首伏羲六經首易而伏羲爲道統
之始合而言之則伏羲信乎爲羣聖民物開物
成務之祖非特文字之祖已也故乾稱父坤稱
punctuated: 行之順布，以至品物之流形，莫非文也，莫非道也。聖人法天以作易，則圖位布列，爻象交錯，寧非所以成天地之文而呈斯道之體哉？故天者，道之祖也；畫者，文之祖也；聖人者，萬世之祖也。由此而書契易焉，甲曆著焉，嫁娶辨焉，衣裳制焉，宮室作焉，朴野變焉，文教興焉。由此而口代天言焉，手代天工焉，心代天意焉，身代天事焉。故謂聖人建天下萬世之極，可也；謂聖人裁成輔相以左右民，亦可也。前乎此者，三皇莫神焉。史稱其澹泊無爲，造化之眞宰未彰，陰陽之氣方孕而未育也。後乎此者，堯舜莫盛焉。史稱其放勳重華，造化之元神已暢，陰陽之氣長養而蕃廡也。包犧氏上繼三皇，應運而生，下開羣聖，撫運而治，故稱乎祖焉。是以論帝系者，以包犧爲五帝之首；著月令者，以太昊爲四時之春；序書言三墳而首伏羲，六經首易而伏羲爲道統之始。合而言之，則伏羲信乎爲羣聖民物開物成務之祖，非特文字之祖已也。故乾稱父，坤稱
translation_en: …the orderly distribution of the Five Phases, extending to the flowing emergence of all things into form: none is without pattern, none without the Way. When the sage modeled himself on Heaven to create the Changes, arranging the positions of the diagrams and interweaving the lines and images, was this not how he completed the pattern of Heaven and Earth and displayed the substance of this Way? Thus Heaven is the progenitor of the Way; the drawn lines are the progenitor of writing; and the sage is the progenitor of all generations. From this came the substitution of written records, the establishment of the cyclical calendar, the distinctions governing marriage, the institution of upper and lower garments, the construction of palaces and dwellings, the transformation of rustic simplicity, and the flourishing of literary and moral instruction. From this, his mouth spoke for Heaven, his hands worked for Heaven, his mind expressed Heaven’s intent, and his person carried out Heaven’s affairs. Thus one may say that the sage established the ultimate standard for all under Heaven and for all generations; one may also say that the sage shaped and completed the work of transformation, assisting it so as to guide the people. Among those who preceded him, none surpassed the Three Sovereigns in spiritual potency. Histories describe them as serene and without deliberate action: the true directing power of creation and transformation had not yet become manifest, and the vital forces of yin and yang were gestating but had not yet come to birth. Among those who followed him, none surpassed Yao and Shun in greatness. Histories describe them as possessing ‘far-reaching achievement’ and ‘renewed splendor’: the primal spirit of creation and transformation had already found full expression, and the vital forces of yin and yang nourished growth and flourished abundantly. Baoxi succeeded the Three Sovereigns before him, being born in response to the destined course of the age; he opened the way for the many sages after him, governing in accordance with that course. Thus he is called the progenitor. Accordingly, those who discuss imperial genealogies place Baoxi first among the Five Emperors; those who composed the Monthly Ordinances associate Taihao with spring among the four seasons. The preface to the Documents speaks of the Three Ancient Records and places Fuxi first; among the Six Classics, the Changes comes first, and Fuxi stands at the beginning of the transmission of the Way. Taken together, these considerations show that Fuxi was indeed the progenitor who opened up the understanding of things and brought undertakings to completion for the many sages, the people, and all beings—not merely the progenitor of writing. Thus Qian is called ‘father,’ and Kun is called…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
母乾坤者大父母也伏羲氏其天地之惟肖乎
使無伏羲則如日之夜如月之晦蠢愚之習喬
野之俗民未知書何以同文民未知禮何以辨
等民未知樂何以和行又安能揚天地之大業
而昭耿光於萬世哉故先儒斷其畫易爲文字
之祖而開萬世人文之治也說者曰酒醴之美
而明水之尚反其本也文繡之美而疏布之尚
貴其質也三皇之世渾樸未鑿民偽未生包犧
氏作八卦制六書視三皇之脩意已不同矣堯
===
舜益之十六字至於六經詳矣何數聖人者遊
心犧皇不欲與天下相安於忘言哉蓋包犧之
世河出天苞所以開文明之漸時也至堯舜則
著矣所謂堯舜通變垂裳而治亦時也若湯文
周孔則時之異為之也數聖人雖欲與斯世同
躋三皇之治不可得矣故曰作易者其有憂患
乎六經之作亦聖人不得已也孔子欲無言而
祖述惟堯舜聖人之意可識矣厥後文字愈繁
而心學愈支太玄潜虛洞極皆所以病易宋儒
punctuated:
母。乾坤者，大父母也。伏羲氏其天地之惟肖乎！使無伏羲，則如日之夜，如月之晦。蠢愚之習，喬野之俗，民未知書，何以同文？民未知禮，何以辨等？民未知樂，何以和行？又安能揚天地之大業，而昭耿光於萬世哉？故先儒斷其畫易爲文字之祖，而開萬世人文之治也。
說者曰：「酒醴之美，而明水之尚，反其本也；文繡之美，而疏布之尚，貴其質也。」三皇之世，渾樸未鑿，民偽未生。包犧氏作八卦，制六書，視三皇之脩意已不同矣。堯舜益之十六字，至於六經詳矣。何數聖人者遊心犧皇，不欲與天下相安於忘言哉？蓋包犧之世，河出天苞，所以開文明之漸，時也；至堯舜則著矣。所謂堯舜通變，垂裳而治，亦時也。若湯文周孔，則時之異為之也。數聖人雖欲與斯世同躋三皇之治，不可得矣。故曰：「作易者，其有憂患乎！」六經之作，亦聖人不得已也。孔子欲無言，而祖述惟堯舜，聖人之意可識矣。厥後文字愈繁，而心學愈支。《太玄》《潜虛》《洞極》皆所以病《易》。宋儒
translation_en:
…mother. Qian and Kun are the great father and mother. How closely Fuxi resembles Heaven and Earth! Without Fuxi, it would be as when the sun gives way to night or the moon disappears at the end of the month. Amid ignorant habits and uncouth customs, if the people did not know writing, how could their script be made uniform? If they did not know ritual, how could distinctions of rank be established? If they did not know music, how could their conduct be harmonized? How, moreover, could they advance the great work of Heaven and Earth and make its brilliant light shine through all ages? Thus earlier Confucian scholars judged that his drawing of the figures of the Changes made him the progenitor of writing and inaugurated government through cultural refinement for all ages.
An interpreter said: “Though wine and sweet liquor are fine, pure water is accorded precedence: this is a return to the source. Though patterned embroidery is fine, coarse cloth is accorded precedence: this honors the plain substance.” In the age of the Three Sovereigns, primordial simplicity had not yet been carved away, and artifice had not yet arisen among the people. Baoxi created the Eight Trigrams and established the six categories of writing; compared with the cultivated intent [?] of the Three Sovereigns, this was already different. Yao and Shun added the sixteen-word teaching, and by the time of the Six Classics the exposition had become detailed. How could these several sages, whose thoughts roamed in the age of Fuxi, not have wished to dwell at ease with all under Heaven in a state where words were forgotten? In Baoxi’s age, however, the Yellow River brought forth the heavenly treasure, thereby beginning the gradual emergence of cultural enlightenment: this was what the times required. By the age of Yao and Shun, it had become manifest. As it is said, Yao and Shun adapted to change and governed with their robes hanging down; this too was what the times required. As for Tang, Wen, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius, differences in their times brought about their actions. Even had these sages wished to raise the world of their day together to the governance of the Three Sovereigns, they could not have done so. Thus it is said: “Did those who composed the Changes have anxieties and troubles?” The composition of the Six Classics likewise arose from circumstances in which the sages had no alternative. Confucius wished to be without words, yet took only Yao and Shun as the models whose ways he transmitted. From this we can understand the sages’ intent. Thereafter, writing grew ever more profuse, while the learning of the mind became ever more fragmented. The Supreme Mystery (Taixuan), Latent Void (Qianxu), and Penetrating the Ultimate (Dongji) all served to impair the Changes. A Song Confucian scholar…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
曰圖雖無文吾終日言不離乎是此可與見易
矣
表
擬宋曾公亮進新唐書表嘉祐五年
馬象乾
同考試官教諭翟批場中多務浮詞此作獨
敷敘典實而忠愛之心油然具見宜錄以式
考試官教諭黃批典則可錄
考試官學正宋批有體制
===
嘉祐五年六月某日具官臣曾公亮謹以
所撰新唐書
上進者伏以
道闡
皇猷昭一代經綸之跡史傳
國是備
九重清暇之觀荷掄選以編摩敢對揚而進
獻臣公亮誠惶誠恐稽首頓首上言竊惟握幾
圖理常重保邦之謨因事納忠貴得資治
punctuated:
曰：「圖雖無文，吾終日言不離乎是。」此可與見易矣。

表
擬宋曾公亮進新唐書表，嘉祐五年。
馬象乾
同考試官教諭翟批：「場中多務浮詞，此作獨敷敘典實，而忠愛之心油然具見，宜錄以式。」
考試官教諭黃批：「典則，可錄。」
考試官學正宋批：「有體制。」

嘉祐五年六月某日，具官臣曾公亮謹以所撰新唐書上進者。伏以道闡皇猷，昭一代經綸之跡；史傳國是，備九重清暇之觀。荷掄選以編摩，敢對揚而進獻。臣公亮誠惶誠恐，稽首頓首上言：竊惟握幾圖理，常重保邦之謨；因事納忠，貴得資治
translation_en:
…said: “Though the diagram contains no writing, nothing I say all day departs from it.” Such a person may be said to have understood the Changes.

Memorial
A memorial in the voice of Zeng Gongliang of the Song dynasty, presenting the New History of the Tang, in the fifth year of Jiayou (1060).
By Ma Xianggan.
Associate Examiner Zhai, Instructor, comments: “Most candidates in this examination devote themselves to empty embellishment. This piece alone sets forth authoritative precedents and historical facts, while its spirit of loyalty and love for the sovereign emerges naturally and fully. It should be recorded as a model.”
Examiner Huang, Instructor, comments: “Classical and correct; worthy of inclusion.”
Examiner Song, School Instructor, comments: “It observes the proper form.”

On a certain day of the sixth month of the fifth year of Jiayou, your servant Zeng Gongliang, holding the requisite offices, respectfully presents the New History of the Tang that he has compiled.

I humbly submit that the Way illuminates imperial counsels, revealing the achievements of a dynasty in ordering the realm; history transmits the guiding principles of the state, providing material for Your Majesty’s perusal in the quiet leisure of the palace. Favored with selection to undertake this compilation, I venture to acknowledge that charge by presenting this work. Your servant Gongliang, with utmost fear and trepidation, bows low and knocks his head upon the ground to submit these words: I humbly consider that discerning the incipient workings of affairs and planning good government always require attention to counsels for preserving the state; offering loyal advice through the events of history requires grasping what can assist in governing…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之要自皇極演於龜範彝訓是陳迄書法
精於麟經勸懲斯備繼有左右史之職廼
爲紀言動之官雖王者能自得師惟
大聖取人爲善顧玆唐紀義切殷盤武德紀元
一朝之得失攸在天祐竣簡歷世之興衰
具存草創于吳兢之文就緒于劉昫之手
但文繁而實則隱致意晦而詞徒多故善
惡不炳於丹青而義例未彰於方冊難仍
舊貫宜創新規玆蓋伏遇
===
神功丕顯
聖德難名
恭儉性成四海樂時雍之治
寬仁天縱八荒懷文德之威
闢黃樞以求言圜青衿而論道謂享國長久
已徵於成周而近代箴規莫切於唐室載
稽往牒爰集衆思董以臣脩而任綜核之
司副以臣祁而嚴考訂之責如臣庸品亦
punctuated:
之要。自皇極演於龜範，彝訓是陳；迄書法精於麟經，勸懲斯備。繼有左右史之職，廼爲紀言動之官。雖王者能自得師，惟大聖取人爲善。顧玆唐紀，義切殷盤。武德紀元，一朝之得失攸在；天祐竣簡，歷世之興衰具存。草創于吳兢之文，就緒于劉昫之手。但文繁而實則隱，致意晦而詞徒多，故善惡不炳於丹青，而義例未彰於方冊。難仍舊貫，宜創新規。
玆蓋伏遇神功丕顯，聖德難名。恭儉性成，四海樂時雍之治；寬仁天縱，八荒懷文德之威。闢黃樞以求言，圜青衿而論道。謂享國長久，已徵於成周；而近代箴規，莫切於唐室。載稽往牒，爰集衆思。董以臣脩，而任綜核之司；副以臣祁，而嚴考訂之責。如臣庸品，亦
translation_en:
…the essentials of aiding government. From the exposition of the August Ultimate in the turtle-inspired Great Plan, enduring precepts were set forth; by the time the principles of historical writing were perfected in the Classic of the Unicorn—the Spring and Autumn Annals—encouragement and admonition were fully provided. There followed the offices of Historiographer of the Left and Historiographer of the Right, officials charged with recording words and deeds. Although a king can himself find a teacher, it is the great sage who draws upon others to do good.
