The questions of urgency and gravity, restraint and release, advance and withdrawal are immediately before our eyes; one need not be wise to understand them. Those who speak of the troubles of the southeast all say that none exceeds the Japanese pirates at sea. These men make boats their homes and order their days by winds and tides. When they gain an advantage, they return; when they suffer a reverse, they flee. Their actions can still be anticipated. The mountain bandits, however, are probably an even graver menace. I, a student, have witnessed their deeds and long harbored indignation. How could I dare not state the facts plainly in reply? May I first set out three reasons why they cannot be pacified, and then proceed to twelve strategies?
What are these reasons? In Zhangzhou in Fujian, Ganzhou in Yuzhang, and Chaozhou and Huizhou in Guangdong, mountains and sea interlace, and the perilous terrain defies reconnaissance. The people are fierce, violent, and crafty, and readily turn to banditry. Even wealthy households willingly serve the various chieftains, answering their calls as promptly as an echo. If anyone tries to correct them, they take up weapons and attack one another: such are their ingrained customs. Recently they have increasingly incited one another to violence, bribing remnants of the Japanese pirates to augment their forces and spreading exaggerated rumors to terrify all who see or hear of them. They have shaken the various prefectures, laying waste wherever they go. Can one bear to speak of the horrors of their cruelties? This is the first reason why they cannot be pacified. Previously, though they charged like boars and darted about like rats, they still feared investigation by the authorities; now, in broad…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
晝橫行絕無忌憚甲子大城相繼被害矣
嶺東一帶戎馬躙蹀民棄室廬委田叢莽
賦稅何所出乎垂涎帑蓄在在戒嚴刁斗
之聲相聞宵達旦矣守土之臣疆場之將
所廢飱以爲備也此二不可撫也我兵勢
强彼不堪窘抑願待不死出自悔心招可
從也今未有挫衂之者乃僅以名通聊懈
官兵之加而身憑險阻肆螫如故有司亦
已揆度蓋拒之則失信激之恐重爲民讎
===
姑羈縻之若與之明誓是立赤幟耳效順
之名何可輕也此三不可撫也當是時不
早爲之處萬一游俠之輩見盜不耕穫不
菑畬子女金帛無所不有終歲勤動何爲
哉亦胥化而爲盜匿山谷聯巢穴牢不可
破大可懼也知乎此則犁掃之責當有慨
然任之者矣兵可易言哉大眾壓境未免
師老匱財間道鵰勦又恐誨之使防而益
長其無忌兵可易用哉前所謂十二略者
punctuated: 晝橫行，絕無忌憚，甲子、大城相繼被害矣。嶺東一帶，戎馬躙蹀，民棄室廬，委田叢莽，賦稅何所出乎？垂涎帑蓄，在在戒嚴，刁斗之聲相聞，宵達旦矣。守土之臣、疆場之將，所廢飱以爲備也。此二不可撫也。我兵勢强，彼不堪窘抑，願待不死，出自悔心，招可從也。今未有挫衂之者，乃僅以名通，聊懈官兵之加，而身憑險阻，肆螫如故。有司亦已揆度，蓋拒之則失信，激之恐重爲民讎，姑羈縻之。若與之明誓，是立赤幟耳。效順之名，何可輕也？此三不可撫也。當是時，不早爲之處，萬一游俠之輩見盜不耕穫、不菑畬，子女金帛無所不有，終歲勤動何爲哉？亦胥化而爲盜，匿山谷，聯巢穴，牢不可破，大可懼也。知乎此，則犁掃之責，當有慨然任之者矣。兵可易言哉？大眾壓境，未免師老匱財；間道鵰勦，又恐誨之使防，而益長其無忌。兵可易用哉？前所謂十二略者，
translation_en:
…they roam at will in broad daylight, utterly without restraint. Jiazi and Dacheng have suffered attacks in succession. Throughout eastern Lingnan, warhorses trample the land; the people abandon their homes and leave their fields to thickets and weeds. Where can tax revenue come from? The bandits covet the treasury reserves, and everywhere is under martial alert. The sound of watchmen striking their bronze cooking vessels carries from post to post, from nightfall until dawn. Officials charged with defending the territory and commanders on the frontiers forgo their meals to make preparations. This is the second reason they cannot be pacified through conciliation.

If our forces were strong and they could no longer endure the pressure, sincerely repented, and hoped to be spared death, an offer of submission could be accepted. Now, however, no one has yet inflicted a defeat upon them. They merely establish contact in name, temporarily easing the pressure of government troops, while relying on difficult terrain and continuing to inflict harm as before. The responsible officials have also weighed the matter: rejecting them would break faith, while provoking them might make them enemies of the people once again. Thus they provisionally keep them under loose restraint. But to enter into a solemn covenant with them would simply be to erect a red banner for them. How can the designation of obedient allegiance be bestowed lightly? This is the third reason they cannot be pacified through conciliation.

At such a time, unless arrangements are made early, what if roving adventurers see that bandits reap without plowing and possess cultivated fields without clearing them, with women, children, gold, and silk—all they could desire? Why, then, toil throughout the year? They too will all turn into bandits, hide in mountain valleys, and link their strongholds into an impregnable network. This is greatly to be feared. Once this is understood, there should be men who resolutely assume responsibility for sweeping them away.

Can military affairs be discussed lightly? Bringing a great army to their borders inevitably risks exhausting the troops and depleting funds. Raids to destroy them by little-used routes [?], meanwhile, may teach them to take precautions and further embolden their recklessness. Can troops be employed lightly? As for the twelve strategies mentioned above…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
願悉其說一曰責守令民皆兵也時簡練
比什伍養之有素矣賊入吾土以身先之
少則戰多則堅壁以守其去也馳報鄰徼
不啻家人父子頃刻雲集腹背夾攻賊雖
强能四面受敵哉有不敎者秦越其民者
也二曰重將領三軍之命繫之一將必士
卒和附方可使蹈湯火投溝壑今提千萬
烏合之兵一旦付之臨陣卽孫武不效也
或軍人或民兵或募丁挑選一千餘人令
===
之操演識名籍馴意氣精藝材稍稍助以
犒賞兼得上下其食以勸義心習之旣熟
能無用命哉三曰協官守石梁之伐兩將
軍異同幾敗乃事三省盜情均之爲民驅
害文移關白如證左券而軍中策應不爽
片時使姦細不得觀望而搖奪語曰衆心
成城况發縱指示乎若泥文墨分比鄰則
非同舟共濟矣四曰嚴信地淮陰之兵不
敢越紀律所恃者信耳今盜一也在山在
punctuated:
願悉其說。一曰責守令。民皆兵也，時簡練，比什伍，養之有素矣。賊入吾土，以身先之；少則戰，多則堅壁以守。其去也，馳報鄰徼，不啻家人父子，頃刻雲集，腹背夾攻。賊雖强，能四面受敵哉？有不敎者，秦越其民者也。
二曰重將領。三軍之命繫之一將，必士卒和附，方可使蹈湯火、投溝壑。今提千萬烏合之兵，一旦付之臨陣，卽孫武不效也。或軍人，或民兵，或募丁，挑選一千餘人，令之操演，識名籍，馴意氣，精藝材，稍稍助以犒賞，兼得上下其食，以勸義心。習之旣熟，能無用命哉？
三曰協官守。石梁之伐，兩將軍異同，幾敗乃事。三省盜情，均之爲民驅害。文移關白，如證左券，而軍中策應不爽片時，使姦細不得觀望而搖奪。語曰：「衆心成城。」况發縱指示乎？若泥文墨，分比鄰，則非同舟共濟矣。
四曰嚴信地。淮陰之兵，不敢越紀律，所恃者信耳。今盜一也，在山在
translation_en:
…I wish to explain these proposals fully.
First: hold prefects and magistrates responsible. The people are all potential soldiers. Select and train them periodically, organize them into groups of ten and five, and maintain them through regular preparation. When bandits enter our territory, lead these men in person. If the bandits are few, fight; if numerous, strengthen the defenses and hold out. When they leave, send swift reports to neighboring jurisdictions. Cooperating as closely as members of a family, fathers and sons, the forces will gather like clouds in an instant and attack from front and rear. Strong though the bandits may be, can they face enemies on all four sides? Officials who fail to train their people treat them as strangers, as remote from one another as Qin and Yue.
Second: give due weight to commanders. The lives of the entire army depend upon a single general. Only when the soldiers are united and devoted to him can he make them tread through boiling water and fire or cast themselves into ditches and ravines. If thousands upon thousands of troops assembled as a disorderly rabble are suddenly entrusted to a commander on the eve of battle, even Sun Wu could accomplish nothing. Select a little over a thousand men, whether regular soldiers, militia, or recruits, and have them drill. Learn their names and rolls, discipline their temperaments and spirit, and refine their skills and abilities. Gradually supplement this with rewards, while also allowing their rations to be increased or decreased to encourage a sense of duty. Once thoroughly trained, how could they fail to obey orders to the utmost?
Third: coordinate officials in their duties. In the campaign against Shiliang, disagreements between the two generals nearly ruined the undertaking. As regards banditry in the three provinces, all share the task of ridding the people of harm. Official communications and notifications should be as verifiable as the matching halves of a contract, and military support should arrive without a moment’s delay, so that spies cannot watch for opportunities to unsettle and undermine our resolve. As the saying goes, “United hearts form a fortress.” How much more does this apply to directing deployments and giving orders? If officials become bogged down in paperwork and draw boundaries between neighboring jurisdictions, they are hardly crossing the river together in the same boat.
Fourth: enforce strict responsibility for assigned posts. The troops of the Marquis of Huaiyin dared not transgress military discipline; what he relied upon was simply the certainty that orders would be upheld. Now the bandits are one and the same, whether in the mountains or in…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
海不可測識官督軍兵各分布扼塞設伏
邀擊官不侵於他委兵勿移之別役如涉
洋登岸賊得自由不知出入即按地覈罪
正以軍法有不股慄哉五曰明應援春秋
之法嘗譏不救地壤相接而坐視勝敗漸
不可長也先期確申期會攻西則擊左東
亦如之攻南則繞後北亦如之攻中左右
前後各起非其守地仗義而至者超格酬
之敢有披靡者哉六曰公賞罰重賞之下
===
必有勇夫罰尤不可廢也廢罰則人不畏
賞罰有成書章章明也亦眾庶共睹者誠
賞不踰時罰不掩耳即入虎穴探虎子利
害鏡於前而敢却步哉何也感則心奮畏
則心寒不待驅也七曰許便宜兵事稱機
言貴神速而賊情呼吸迅於鳥舉必俟批
答而行則動經閱月能披堅以聽哉糧餉
轉輓屬之當道一聞警急將領挺身赴之
少假文法作其銳氣事寧甄別未為晚也
punctuated:
海，不可測識。官督軍兵，各分布扼塞，設伏邀擊。官不侵於他委，兵勿移之別役。如涉洋登岸，賊得自由，不知出入，即按地覈罪，正以軍法，有不股慄哉？
五曰明應援。《春秋》之法，嘗譏不救。地壤相接，而坐視勝敗，漸不可長也。先期確申期會，攻西則擊左，東亦如之；攻南則繞後，北亦如之；攻中，左右前後各起。非其守地，仗義而至者，超格酬之，敢有披靡者哉？
六曰公賞罰。重賞之下，必有勇夫，罰尤不可廢也。廢罰則人不畏。賞罰有成書，章章明也，亦眾庶共睹者。誠賞不踰時，罰不掩耳，即入虎穴探虎子，利害鏡於前，而敢却步哉？何也？感則心奮，畏則心寒，不待驅也。
七曰許便宜。兵事稱機，言貴神速，而賊情呼吸迅於鳥舉。必俟批答而行，則動經閱月，能披堅以聽哉？糧餉轉輓，屬之當道；一聞警急，將領挺身赴之。少假文法，作其銳氣，事寧甄別，未為晚也。
translation_en:
…at sea, their whereabouts cannot be ascertained. Officials should supervise the troops, deploying them separately to hold strategic passes, lay ambushes, and intercept the enemy. Officials should not be diverted to other assignments, nor should troops be transferred to other duties. If the bandits are allowed to cross the sea and land at will, their movements going undetected, investigate culpability according to the area of responsibility and punish those responsible under military law. Would anyone fail to tremble?
Fifth: clarify arrangements for mutual support. The principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals condemn failures to come to another’s rescue. Where territories adjoin, the practice of sitting by and watching others win or lose must not be allowed to grow. Firmly reiterate in advance the appointed times for coordinated action. When an attack is made in the west, strike the left flank; do likewise in the east. When an attack is made in the south, circle around to the rear; do likewise in the north. When an attack is made in the center, let forces on the left, right, front, and rear all rise into action. Those who come out of a sense of duty, even though the area is outside their assigned defense sector, should receive rewards beyond the normal scale. Would anyone dare to give way?
Sixth: make rewards and punishments impartial. Generous rewards are sure to bring forth brave men, but punishment is particularly indispensable. If punishment is abandoned, people will have no fear. There are established written regulations for rewards and punishments, clear and explicit, which everyone can see. If rewards are truly granted without delay and punishment comes before one can cover one’s ears, then even when entering a tiger’s den to seize its cubs, with benefits and dangers reflected plainly before them, would men dare to retreat? Why is this? Gratitude rouses the heart, while fear chills it: there is no need to drive them forward.
Seventh: permit discretion in taking expedient action. Military affairs must suit the opportunity; as the saying goes, extraordinary speed is essential. The bandit situation changes in a breath, faster than a bird takes flight. If action must always await a written reply, a month can easily pass. Can men remain clad in armor waiting for orders? Entrust the transport of provisions and military funds to the authorities in charge. As soon as an emergency is reported, commanders should personally hasten to the scene. Allow them some latitude in procedural requirements to rouse their fighting spirit. Once the trouble has been settled, it will not be too late to assess their conduct.

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
閫外之令一切不令撓之俾得從容畫策
吾但責之以成庸無次第可觀者哉八曰
開糾擿漢時青徐幽冀盜發詔令自相糾
擿五人共斬一人除其罪未幾卽解賊苦
兵革與之更生有不踴躍而應乎果不昵
夙好從中自戕但具首級以告亦除之獲
酋長者充上賞約如金石彼此遞效黨類
疑怯或可乗而定也九曰用間諜古之賢
將不愛千金能使人出萬死以間敵國幸
===
與不幸之間彼往者善探陰計灼見虛實
使我得靜以制彼卽畀上爵亦不爲過何
惜千金也十曰懲納賄虞受璧乗卒失下
陽貪小僨大也賊計詭譎往往賄間兵官
擁胄旁觀逗遛不至賊勝諉之力薄賊不
勝徉示歸徑縱之逸去此故態也有若人
焉立徇之法恐諸葛不能赦馬謖矣十一
曰原脅從書云殲厥渠魁脅從罔治彼被
虜者肯捐親戚擲墳墓而甘心從盜哉大
punctuated:
閫外之令，一切不令撓之，俾得從容畫策，吾但責之以成庸，無次第可觀者哉？
八曰：開糾擿。漢時青徐幽冀盜發，詔令自相糾擿，五人共斬一人，除其罪，未幾卽解。賊苦兵革，與之更生，有不踴躍而應乎？果不昵夙好，從中自戕，但具首級以告，亦除之。獲酋長者充上賞，約如金石，彼此遞效，黨類疑怯，或可乗而定也。
九曰：用間諜。古之賢將不愛千金，能使人出萬死以間敵國。幸與不幸之間，彼往者善探陰計，灼見虛實，使我得靜以制彼，卽畀上爵亦不爲過，何惜千金也？
十曰：懲納賄。虞受璧乗，卒失下陽，貪小僨大也。賊計詭譎，往往賄間兵官，擁胄旁觀，逗遛不至。賊勝，諉之力薄；賊不勝，徉示歸徑，縱之逸去，此故態也。有若人焉，立徇之法，恐諸葛不能赦馬謖矣。
十一曰：原脅從。書云：「殲厥渠魁，脅從罔治。」彼被虜者，肯捐親戚、擲墳墓，而甘心從盜哉？大
translation_en:
…As for commands in the field, allow no interference whatsoever, so that the commander may devise his plans at leisure. We need only hold him responsible for accomplishing the task. Would there then be no visible progress?
Eighth: encourage mutual denunciation. During the Han, when bandits arose in Qing, Xu, You, and Ji, an edict ordered them to expose one another: if five men jointly beheaded one, their crimes would be pardoned. Before long, the bands dispersed. The bandits suffer from warfare; if offered a fresh start, would any fail to respond eagerly? If they truly abandon their attachment to former associates and kill someone within their own ranks, they too should be pardoned upon presenting the severed head and reporting the deed. Those who capture a chief should receive the highest reward. With these pledges as firm as metal and stone, they will emulate one another in succession, and their confederates will grow suspicious and fearful. We may then be able to exploit this and pacify them.
Ninth: employ spies. The worthy generals of antiquity did not begrudge a thousand pieces of gold and could induce men to brave countless mortal dangers to spy on enemy states. With success and failure hanging in the balance, if those sent out skillfully uncover secret plans and clearly discern the enemy’s weaknesses and strengths, enabling us to control him while remaining at rest, even granting them the highest rank of nobility would not be excessive. Why begrudge a thousand pieces of gold?
Tenth: punish the acceptance of bribes. Yu accepted a jade disk and a team of horses, and ultimately lost Xiayang: greed for a small gain brought a great ruin. The bandits’ schemes are deceitful. They often bribe military officers to subvert them; these officers stand by with their helmets on, watching, or delay and fail to arrive. If the bandits prevail, they plead insufficient strength; if the bandits lose, they feign an indication of a route of retreat [?], letting them escape. This is their habitual conduct. Should there be such a man, immediately apply the law of public execution to him. I fear that even Zhuge Liang could not pardon Ma Su.
Eleventh: pardon those coerced into joining. The Book of Documents says: “Destroy their ringleaders; do not punish those compelled to follow.” Would those taken captive willingly abandon their relatives and forsake their ancestral graves, gladly joining the bandits? The great army…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
兵所向首開自新來者鞫無異狀收錄幕
下資為嚮道老幼無依者還之鄉里此風
一聞賊雖結之以恩必不忍自納於死矣
十二曰謹接濟米粟硝黃賊所仰需於人
者價高數等冒禁交易暮夜掩襲誰則詰
之若置而不問是借寇兵而齎盜糧非計
之完也峻其防於守隘之官而犯者盡法
不貰法重於利彼忍殞命而不顧哉是故
責守令而民可使也重將領而兵可制也
===
協官守而事可圖也嚴信地而志可固也
明應援而心可齊也公賞罰而勇可倡也
許便宜而令可施也開糾擿而勢可孤也
用間諜而情可燭也懲納賄而威可振也
原脅從而黨可攜也謹接濟而命可握也
由是宣布
聖明之威靈申播
祖宗之德澤受節制於兩鎮紀功績於憲臣然
後行事如雷霆之震疾不可犯如鬼神之
banxin: 山東鄉試錄 九十四
punctuated:
兵所向，首開自新，來者鞫無異狀，收錄幕下，資為嚮道；老幼無依者，還之鄉里。此風一聞，賊雖結之以恩，必不忍自納於死矣。
十二曰謹接濟。米粟硝黃，賊所仰需於人者，價高數等，冒禁交易，暮夜掩襲，誰則詰之？若置而不問，是借寇兵而齎盜糧，非計之完也。峻其防於守隘之官，而犯者盡法不貰。法重於利，彼忍殞命而不顧哉？
是故責守令而民可使也，重將領而兵可制也，協官守而事可圖也，嚴信地而志可固也，明應援而心可齊也，公賞罰而勇可倡也，許便宜而令可施也，開糾擿而勢可孤也，用間諜而情可燭也，懲納賄而威可振也，原脅從而黨可攜也，謹接濟而命可握也。由是宣布聖明之威靈，申播祖宗之德澤，受節制於兩鎮，紀功績於憲臣，然後行事如雷霆之震，疾不可犯；如鬼神之
translation_en:
…wherever the army advances, first offer an opportunity to reform. Those who come forward and reveal nothing suspicious under interrogation should be enrolled under the command staff and employed as guides. The elderly and young who have no one to support them should be returned to their home villages. Once word of this policy spreads, even if the bandits have bound them through favors, they will surely be unwilling to consign themselves to death.
The twelfth point is to exercise strict vigilance over supplies reaching the bandits. Rice, grain, saltpeter, and sulfur are things the bandits depend on others to supply. Prices several times higher induce people to violate prohibitions and trade with them, making covert incursions by night [?]—who will investigate them? To leave this unchecked is to lend weapons to the enemy and furnish provisions to robbers; it is no comprehensive strategy. Require the officials guarding the passes to enforce strict controls, and punish offenders to the full extent of the law without pardon. When the penalties outweigh the profits, would they willingly lose their lives without a second thought?
Thus, hold prefects and magistrates accountable, and the people can be mobilized; give weight to military commanders, and the troops can be controlled; coordinate officials in their duties, and undertakings can be planned; enforce strict observance of assigned defense sectors, and resolve can be secured; clarify arrangements for mutual support, and hearts can be united; make rewards and punishments impartial, and courage can be encouraged; permit discretionary action, and orders can be carried out; open channels for reporting and exposing wrongdoing, and the bandits’ power can be isolated; employ spies, and the actual circumstances can be illuminated; punish the acceptance of bribes, and authority can be strengthened; pardon those coerced into joining, and the bandits’ following can be divided; exercise vigilance over their supplies, and their fate can be held in our hands. In this way, proclaim the awe-inspiring might of our sagely sovereign and spread anew the beneficence of the imperial ancestors. Receive direction from the two regional commanders, and have achievements recorded by the censorial officials. Then act like the thunder’s peal, so swift that none can withstand it; like the spirits’…

title: 嘉靖四十年廣東鄉試錄
text:
運秘不可窺功收萬全在此一舉蕞爾山
寇何足平哉酋之所獲以俘以
獻地之所復以寨以堡四郊銷多壘之患百姓
安耕鑿之常神人之憤已紓
國家之祜益篤海隅蒼生何其幸歟不是之
務而徒規規於撫譬之患癰疽者勢已迫
矣不付醫手而聽其自潰其如身何書生
常談或可以效安攘之助惟執事采焉
punctuated: 運秘不可窺，功收萬全，在此一舉。蕞爾山寇，何足平哉！酋之所獲，以俘以獻；地之所復，以寨以堡。四郊銷多壘之患，百姓安耕鑿之常，神人之憤已紓，國家之祜益篤。海隅蒼生，何其幸歟！不是之務，而徒規規於撫，譬之患癰疽者，勢已迫矣，不付醫手，而聽其自潰，其如身何？書生常談，或可以效安攘之助，惟執事采焉。
translation_en:
…their mysterious workings cannot be fathomed. Complete success rests on this single undertaking. What difficulty could there be in subduing these paltry mountain bandits? Let the captured chieftains be presented as prisoners, and let stockades and forts be established on the recovered land. The countryside on every side will be freed from the scourge of hostile encampments, and the common people will peacefully resume their accustomed ploughing and well-digging. The indignation of spirits and men will be assuaged, and the blessings upon the state will grow still greater. How fortunate the people of this coastal region will be!

To neglect this task and instead concern oneself narrowly with pacification is like someone suffering from an abscess: the condition has already become critical, yet he does not entrust himself to a physician, but lets it burst on its own. What will become of his body? These commonplace remarks of a scholar may perhaps contribute to securing peace within and repelling threats from without. I ask only that you, sir, consider adopting them.
